Washington, D.C., Feb. 3, 1912.-Senators who discussed the symposium giving the views of shipping men and exporters on cana-l tolls, said the question of tolls should be soon settled .
Senator Brandeger, chairman of the Senate Committee on Interoceanic Canals, said that he was emphatically in favour of rebating the tolls paid by American ships. ' American shipping interests,' he said, 'should be encouraged to use the canal to develop our foreign trade.'
Senator Penrose said: ' The canal is not alone a war measure, but is an industrial project which is expected to advance the commercial -interests of the United States. the United States passing through the canal. The proposal in the despatch which I have read is to give a rebate to American ships in order to encourage American commerce. 1 Has the government received the following resolution unanimously adopted by the Board of Trade of Montreal at its annual meeting held on Wednesday the 31st January ultimo:
' That this board views with alarm the exploiting by corporation or individuals of the waters of the St. Lawrence for power purposes, and that in view of the fact that the city of Montreal is the centre of a district which is capable of more water-power development than most other cities in the world, it should have the advantage thereof in the shape of low electric power rates, which are so essential to the growth of a city and to have full development of its manufacturing industries;
' This board is of the opinion that before the Dominion Government sanctions the various schemes now being put forward for the development of hydro-electric power on both the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers, it is essential in the interest of the country generally that the conservation commission should he requested to draw up a comprehensive scheme for the preservation of these rivers as great national waterways of the Dominion, and that such commission should take immediate action so as to prevent the natural resources of the publio domain from passing into the hands of private parties;
'That the Dominion Government is hereby prayed to instruct the Conservation Commission to consider what means it is advisable to adopt, first in regard to the licensing of hvdro-electric companies; second what check it is desirable to put on the increases in the capital of the various companies in order that some means may he evolved for giving the

public electric power at a minimum rate, yet at the same time allowing the various electrical companies to make a reasonable return for their shareholders on the paid-up capital: third, to prevent, if possible, such companies making unwarranted increases in their capital stock on the basis of earnings: and fourth, to consider whether a Hydro-Electric Commission should be established by the Dominion Government to govern rates of power companies on a similar basis to the Board of Railwav Commissioners, or whether it would serve the public interest better for the government to itself develop hydro-electric power and distribute the same on lines similar to those of the Hydro-Electric Commission in Ontario;	. ,

He said:	Mr. Speaker, in making this
motion, I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or in his absence, that of the Prime Minister, to the importance of dealing with this question. On the 6th of February of last year I had the honour to move in this House a resolution in regard to this matter, as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, as the mode of fishing known as steam trawling, prosecuted by ships of different nationalities on the coast of Canada outside Canadian waters, is destructive to fish life, it is expedient, in order to conserve the deep sea fisheries, that negotiations be opened with the view of securing an international agreement prohibiting steam trawling on such fish-1 dug grounds for deep sea fish, as the waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the hanks of the North Atlantic adjacent to the coasts of Canada and Newfoundland.
That-resolution was passed by the House, last session and I understand that negotiations were opened by the late government with certain foreign powers and with the British government, looking towards some action which would carry out the views expressed in that resolution. The late government did considerable in the way of discouraging this mode of fishing on the Canadian coasts. Very shortly after the first trawlers appeared on the coasts of Canada, an order in council was passed prohibiting steam trawlers from fishing in Canadian waters, which of course include all the bays, harbours and coast lines of Canada on both the Atlantic and the Pacific. It is contended by the fishermen that this mode of fishing is very disastrous to their interests and very destructive of fish life. The facts in relation to the question were laid pretty fully before the House in the
discussion which took place last year, so that I do not intend to repeat them. However, the step to which I have alluded was taken by the late government to prohibit that mode of fishing in Canadian [DOT]waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: While the subject is practically a new one to me, it is well worthy of consideration, and I shall consult with the officials especially charged with the duty of protecting the fisheries with a view to protecting 'the interests of our fishermen.

I am afraid the minister has not realized the great importance of this question to the fishermen. Holding the views that he does in regard t-o it I would be afraid he would not take any very extreme or active steps in order to prohibit this mode of fishing in Canadian waters. I would refer the minister to a discussion which took place last year when proofs were adduced that this mode of fishing is really destructive to fish life, and that it is impossible for the line and net fishermen to carry on business in the same waters with a steam trawler. I would not like to accept the theory that steam trawling has not injured the fishing in the North Sea. My view is that it has. Investigations have been held in Great Britain and there is a great deal of literature on the question. The British government have gone so far as to employ trawlers of their own to operate in the North Sea and have tabulated the results, showing the large quantities of small and immature fish caught bv the trawlers that had to be thrown overboard because they were too small to be placed on the market. Evidence of that kind was placed on 'Hansard' last session.
This mode of fishing lias only commenced in the United States. The theory prevailed for many years that the bottom of the sea on the coasts of the United States

and Canada were too rough to enable trawlers to operate in our waters. Only a few days ago I received a copy of a resolution moved by Mr. Gardner, of Massachusetts, in the Congress at Washington in regard to this matter. The resolution reads:
Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled.
1. That the Commissioner of Fisheries be, and he is hereby authorized and directed to make an investigation into the method of fishing known as beam trawling and to report to Congress whether or not this method of fishing is destructive to the fish species or is otherwise harmful or undesirable.
Sec. 2. That in the event that the Commissioner of Fisheries finds this method of fishing to be destructive, harmful, or undesirable he shall recommend to Congress such legislation as he may deem necessary.
Sec. 3. That an appropriation is hereby authorized for carrying into effect the provisions of this resolution.
Thus it will be seen that this is a live question in the United States, and in Washington last year I found a great deal of interest taken in it by members of Congress representing districts along the coast. As far as I could judge the sympathy was altogether in favour of standing by the shore fishermen and prohibiting trawling altogether on the coast of the United States. If my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) will continue the correspondence that has been opened with Washington, he will find a good deal of sympathy there in regard to the abolition of this mode of fishing on the coast. It is only now when it is commencing that it can be stopped. If it is true that it has been destructive in the North sea, it should certainly be stopped here before it becomes established, and before large amounts of capital are invested in it.
I do not wish to make this a controversial question, although certain members of the opposition last year-now on the Speaker's right did endeavour to raise trouble about it in that way; but I will say to my hon. friend that if he can devise any means of dealing with this question, I feel that I can say for my colleagues on this side of the House that he will have their cordial support.

speechtext:
For a copy of all papers, correspondence and reports between Capt. Newcombe and the Marine and Fishery Department, relating to the patrol and protection service for fisheries on the Pacific coast?
He said: This is not the first time that this subject has been before the House. In 1906 when I had the honour of being a member of this House, the question of the protection of the fisheries of the Domin-Mr. SINCLAIR.
ion, and especially of the Pacific coast, wras under discussion. To my mind, this is a very important question, and worthy of the most careful consideration of the House. The fisheries of this Dominion, and especially of the Pacific coast, are of exceeding value.
1 find that last year the fisheries of the whole Dominion were valued at $29,629,169. Of that sum the fisheries of the Pacific coast contributed $10,314,755, considerably over one-third of the total value of all the fisheries of the Dominion. What I want especially to draw attention to is the inadequate patrol service that is given on the Pacific coast, especially in British Columbia. I understand that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is fully alive to this question, and I sincerely trust that he will see that a proper protection service is placed upon that coast, sufficient to - protect adequately this great national asset. I think that every hon. member of this House who is aware of the conditions will admit that there is, and has been for a number of years past, a very inadequate service provided on that coast. It was in 1904, I think, that the first urgent demand was made for a protective service. In 1906 it appears that there were 52 foreign vessels poaching in waters that rightly belong to this Dominion, and it is estimated that they made an illegal catch of 41,664,329 lbs. of fish, which is valued at 5 cents a lb. I want the House to understand that 1 am now especially referring to halibut fishing on that coast.' The value of fish caught that I have already mentioned, is estimated at $2,083,216. In 1906 we find that over 200 foreign vessels, that is, other than Rritish or Canadian bottoms, were poaching in those waters, and it is estimated that the average catch since then has been 65,000,000 lbs. to say nothing about the possible 20,000,000, or 25,000,0(10 lbs. of edible fish which are thrown away and do not reach the markets. I think these figures will convince the House of the great importance of this question, and I trust they will interest every hon. member, whether he represents a fishing district or not. It is, I say, a national asset of very great importance, which the government ought to use every endeavour adequately to protect.
Now the boats which are chartered for this fishery protective service are absolutely inadequate for thei purpose. They1 are boats which do not make more than eight or ten knots an hour, and they are not properly equipped to cope with the up-to-date boats that are employed in the poaching business. These latter boats are well equipped with wireless, whereby they may keep in touch with each other, and are able to evade the protective service that has been paid for by this government during the last two or three years. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will

see to it that we have at least three thoroughly up-to-date steamers employed on that service, steamers which are able to make at least 15 to 18 knots an hour, thoroughly equipped with wireless, and able to cope successfully with the illegal fishing. Now I do not propose to go back and discuss the different treaties governing this fishing. I understand that the treaty of 1818 which gives us our proper rights and that it yt as only in 1909 that it was pu-t into force, I think the treaty of 1818 ought to he henceforth rigorously carried out, but to my mind the service that has been employed on that coast for the last two or three years has not mended matters a particle. "
Prior to that treaty being enforced our own Canadian fishermen were allowed to catch and sell bait to the foreign fishermen who were then coming into our waters. As it is now, without any protection on the coast of British Columbia, these poachers come in and immediately set about preparing their nets and other equipment to catch their own bait in our bays and inlets and with that bait they catch fish in our waters. My own personal opinion is that, with boats properly equipped, the fishery protection service should not be under the control of the navy. It should be a separate service and the officers in charge of the vessels should be guided by their own judgment and not be hampered by a command to be at a certain point at a certain time. With a proper service these foreign boats that are now poaching would be absolutely driven from our Canadian waters and put out of business. I sincerely trust that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see that a vote is placed in the estimates for a service to assist in protecting British subjects in the enjoyment of the fisheries of our own waters. If these poachers are not allowed to fish illegally within the three mile limit, if they are driven from our bays so that they cannot clean, dress and pack their fish, they will be absolutely put out of business. It will take a good deal of money to equip a fleet of steamers for this protective service, but when you consider the importance of this great asset and the fact that British Columbia is contributing more than a third of the total product of the fisheries of this Dominion, I think you will admit that it is a service that ought to be equipped at the earliest possible moment. I have much pleasure in stating to the House that I understand the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is thoroughly alive to the importance of this question. There is one other matter in connection with that service which I think is very important, and that has reference to the establishment and operation of wireless telegraph stations along the coast. I understand that at the present time wireless stations are under the control of the naval service. I think it would be much better if that policy were changed and if proper wireless stations were equipped along the coast, not altogether as an aid to the fishery protection service, but from the public standpoint as well as from the protective standpoint. I do not wish to detain the House because I know that my associates from British Columba are far more conversant with this vast subject than I am. I am only speaking from the knowledge which I have gained from having resided in British Columbia, and from what I have learned as to the extent and importance of the fisheries there, and I can only repeat that I sincerely trust that this House, and especially the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, will give this very important question carefu'l consideration. If time would permit I would take up the consideration of the salmon, herring, and other fisheries of that province, but I do not propose to discuss them at the present moment. 1 think that many suggestions could be offered to the minister with respect to the fisheries other than the halibut fishery to which I have especially referred in my remarks.
There are many things that could be done in the interests of our own actual fislier-_ men. The legislation which has been en-' forced during the last few years has operated greatly to the detriment of white, Canadian fishermen in that province and some very drastic change must be made if we want to ensure to the actual, white fisherman, the rights to Which he is entitled and which he does not enjoy at the present time. It is not in the interest of this Dominion, or of .the province, that Japs should engage in the fisheries in the manner in which they are now permitted to do. I could give you many reasons for that opinion, but the question is such a broad one that it would take many hours to discuss it. But, they are depriving the actual white fisherman in that province of his rights.

censes 'are to-day granted to actual white fishermen, but, they do not control those licenses. They are controlled by corporations, but, while I believe that vested interests should be protected, I also believe that the white fisherman, the fisherman who pulls an oar, should have the right to catch and sell fish to the oanners or in the market which will give him the best value for it. He does not have that right to-day, especially in the waters of the Pacific coast. I should like to go on and discuss many other items in connection with this question, but I know that my associates who have lived in the province for many years and who are more familiar with it than I am, will have something to say with regard to it and therefore I do not propose to say very much more on the subject. I only trust that the minister will give every consideration to the remarks which I have addressed to the House this afternoon on this very important question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is a question in which I have taken an active interest, I would not like to have a vote taken upon the resolution without saying a word or two in corroboration of what has been stated by my hon. friend from Coinox-Atlin (Mr. Clements).
He has covered all the ground so far as the question of poaching is concerned so fully that there is very little that I can add. That poaching exists and has existed for a number of years, and that it has existed unchecked can hardly be denied. It has become so open, that it is a common thing to take up a daily newspaper, published in the city of Seattle in the state of Washington, and to find there items reporting the catches taken by American vessels along the coast of British Columbia, and in particular on the coast of Vancouver island. It is also an ordinary thing to read in the American newspapers that -certain vessels are being constructed for the express purpose of going into this business. It has become also common to read the reports of the officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department saying that they are unquestionably unable, with the means at their command, to cope with this abuse. It is common to find the passenger steamers engaged in the coasting trade along the shores of British Columbia coming into port and reporting that they had seen here and there in the different ports along the coast numbers of American vessels using Canadian harbours. It was stated on one occasion, I remember, by the captain of one of these coasting vessels, that the lights of the American fishing schooners in one of the ports of Vancouver island seemed like the lights in the streets of a city. In addition to this, the poachers have become so bold that last year they actually at the Mr. CLEMENTS.
point of the rifle drove the men off the Canadian salmon traps and stole the fish. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is not a nice sort of thing for Canadians to contemplate. Of course, altogether apart from the wasteful methods of these poachers, it puts the people of the province of British Columbia and the people of the whole Dominion in a humiliating position to think that they have a valuable asset in the fisheries of that coast which they are unable to protect. I may say, apropos of the wasteful methods of these poachers that it is a fact that in numbers of eases the halibut beds are being rapidly depleted and that the average size of the fish has dropped from about one hundred pounds to twenty pounds. Now so far as I can ascertain there have been no efforts on the part of the government of Canada to protect the Pacific coast fisheries. The steamer ' Kestrel ' which has now been scrapped was until last summer the vessel upon which the department directly relied for the prevention of this poaching. Well, Mr. Speaker, you might as well try to catch a canary bird by putting salt on its tail as to try to catch one of these gasoline poachers with the ' Kestrel.' During the past six or seven years there have been I think, only three or four of these vtssels caught, notwithstanding the fact that poaching has become a regular line of trade, in the neighbourhood of the city of Seattle, and the ports of Puget Sound, in British Columbia waters. About two years ago a vessel called the ' Levi Woodbury,' was seized and condemned, and I am advised on pretty good authority that she was afterwards released by the late government on payment of a fine of $50, because the vessel was reported to be owned by a friend of the then administration. In addition to the ' Kestrel ' there are one or two smau boats engaged for the ostensible purpose of preventing poaching, and there have been from time to time a couple of whaling boats chartered in addition to a boat called the 'William Joliffe,' but all of these are absolutely unfit for the purpose they are intended for. Since 1907, the year it may be remembered before the general election, there has been an appropriation annually in the estimates for the building of a fishery protection cruiser, but no fishery protection cruiser has ever materialized. The late administration seemed to be somewhat of the opinion that that item in the estimates was going to prevent our American friends from taking the fish, but curiously enough it has not had that effect. Now, Mr, Speaker, I want to say to this House that these fisheries are worth protecting. Professor Prince has made a report on the Pacific coast fisheries, in which he says they are probably the finest fisheries belonging to any one country anywhere in the world. He also says that they

are unique in regard to the fact that they are wholly within protected waters, and that they can be operated with more safety and less loss of life than is experienced in connection with the fisheries on the Atlantic coast. That shows, Sir, that these fisheries are an asset which it is well worth our while protecting. I venture to say that the cost of properly protecting these fisheries will be more than amply repaid by the saving to the country in the fish which would otherwise be poached. I am glad to see that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has provided in the estimates for this year for the building of two or more cruisers. I would like to impress on him the absolute necessity there is for getting these cruisers into commission as soon as possible. I would also suggest to him that these cruisers be built in the province of British Columbia, if that can be done. I do not see any reason why they should not be built in that province. We find that the Canadian Pacific railway, and other large concerns are building vessels in British Columbia, and there can be no reason why the Dominion government should not also do so. It may be said that it would cost a little more to build a vessel on the Pacific coast than in this part of Canada. I would point out that the late administration did not find that an objection, for they were committed to the principle of encouraging shipbuilding in Canada even though they had to pay more than if the ships were built in the old country. In connection with their naval policy, when they called for tenders for the ships it was provided that they should be built in Canada, although they would probably cost thirty per cent more than if built in England. If it is a good thing for Canada that we should pay this increased cost for the benefit of having ships built on the Atlantic coast, it would be equally good for the country to have these ships built on the Pacific coast, so as to establish the industry there, even though they should cost fifty per cent more. I trust the minister will at a very early date give out the contracts for these fishery protection cruisers, and that when he does so he will endeavour to have them built in British Columbia.
Mr. H, H. STEVENS (Vancouver). Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements), for bringing this question before the House. It is a very important and burning question on the Pacific coast. We have felt very keenly the inattention and negligence of the former administration in reeard to our deep-sea fisheries, and wish to take advantage of this opportunity to place ourselves on record, as supporters of the government, in favour of adequate protection for those fisheries. The natural physical features of the Pacific coast lend themselves to the abuse of this great industry, particularly to poaching. At the present time poaching is carried on to such an extent that we might almost as well have our fisheries under the control of our American friends in Puget Sound. Between two and three hundred American boats leave Puget Sound constantly to fish in our waters, whereas our own fishermen have only six or seven. This could not be, but for the fact that, by our policy, we permit American fishermen to receive shelter, to purchase bait, to clean their fish, and to do other things necessary to the life of the industry. Were we to enforce the law as it should be enforced, very few of these boats could fish in our waters, because they would be too far from their ports to carry on the business successfully. As you know, it is necessary for the fishing boats, especially those engaged in the halibut industry, to go into harbour to put their fish in shape, owing to the stormy nature of the sea. This great fishing industry of the Pacific coast belongs peculiarly to the Canadian pieople, and I believe our laws should be enforced in such a way as to protect the interests of our own people in that industry. Reference has already been made to. the kind of protection we have at present. We have two old boats, the ' Quadra ' and the ' Kestrel/ which are the laughing stock of the fishing people of the Pacific coast. They never were adequate, they never had any speed, they have never been able to catch up to the average fishing boat on the coast. Consequently, as years went by, the American fishermen came to ignore entirely the presence of these fishery cruisers, or protectors, as they are falsely called. What we require on the Pacific coast is at least three fairly large fishery cruisers of a type similar to that of the American fishing boats, of 100 tons burden, and of a speed of at least 15 knots an hour. If we had boats of that type it would not be long before the poachers would find their business to be so unprofitable that they would leave our fisheries alone. We should also have stationed at all the harbours along the coast, where these American boats are wont to come, a number of officials who could advise the cruisers what boats had been illegally in any of these harbours. It would cost very little to have these officials, and I recommend it to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. There are men living at these harbours who have other means of support, and who would be willing, for $12 or $15 a month, to watch these American poachers, and give information concerning them. This fishery protection service should be placed under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the fishery superintendent. I understand that at the present time it is under

coast, the history of the industry is reversed, for the production rose from 6,877,640 pounds in 1899, to 21,706,000 pounds in 1909, over [DOT]welve times the total Atlantic catch. The bulk of the halibut fishing is done by vessels outfitted at Seattle and Tacoma, in the State of Washington, but a great deal of their fishing is done in Canadian water, notably in Hecate strait.
It is a disputed point between the Canadian and Amerioan authorities whether Hecate strait is neutral or Canadian water. We claim it is Canadian water. But the Dominion government some years ago granted a privilege to the New England Fish Company, an American corporation, which practically admits that Hecate strait is neutral or open water. They granted to this company the privilege of shipping its fish through Canadian ports in bond to the eastern markets. The reason the New England Fish Company wanted that privilege was, that if they could run into Vancouver they were fifteen hours nearer the American market than at Seattle. This is a great advantage. It will be realized at once that in the transportation of fresh fish this is an advantage that should be reserved to the Canadian people to whom it by right belongs. It has been claimed by supporters of the late government that this concession was distinctly an advantage to Vancouver. I contend it is not because this fishing company have been able to control the market to such an extent that the Canadian fishermen have not been able to go into the fishing business in Vancouver. I will explain how this is brought about. When the New England Fish Company bring fish into Vancouver the choice fish is shipped to the American markets, but in fishing for heavy fish, like halibut, there is always some soft or bruised fish which it is impossible to ship to the eastern market, these fish are dumped on the local market. Hon. members will say that, according to the regulations, they are not permitted to sell in Vancouver or on the local market. To overcome that they place these inferior fish in cars, and bill them out to Bellingham. But in many cases the cars would not leave Vancouver. The freight and duty would be paid and then they would be sold in the market at Vancouver as A-l fish. In some cases, these fish are actually sent out of the country, but they are shipped back in the same oars. This practice has gone on for many years. If this privilege had not been granted to the New England Fish Company, Canadian companies would, have sprung up who could have shipped fish through as the New England Fish Company does to the markets on the Atlantic coast. It is true they would have had to pay a duty of a cent a pound on going into the American mar-Mr. STEVENS.
kets, but my contention is that the natural advantage we enjoy on the Pacific coast, if the laws were enforced, would more than offset the one cent a pound duty. We have a great natural advantage in having our harbours 15 hours nearer the market, and this more than offsets the handicap of a one-eent per pound duty. So I say that the regulation or privilege that was extended to the New England Fish Company is inimical to the best interests of the Canadian fishermen on the Pacific coasts, and I trust that the Minister of Marine and the present government will see their way clear to cancel that permit and to secure a more thorough enforcement of the laws on the Pacific coast.
I wish to say a few words on the whaling industry of the Pacific coast. This is also a most profitable industry. I am quite aware that whaling must be carried on on the high seas, but if whales can be caught contiguous to a whaling station, it stands to reason, they can be handled more profitably than if they had to be carried several hundreds or thousands of miles. On the Pacific coast we have had considerable returns from the whaling inindustry. I have here in this report of the British Columbia government, a recommendation to which I would call the attention of the Dominion government.
Whalers, operating in the sea of Japan and Behring sea, do a considerable trade in whale meat, which is extensively used for food in Japan. Instead of converting the ' beef ' into fertilizer it is salted and in this form commands a better price. The importation of whale meat into Japan amounts to over two million pounds annually, representing a value of over $50,000. Pickled whales* tails are estimated a delicacy in Japan, and large quantities are shipped from this coast.
About two-thirds of the whales captured are cow-whales, either with suckling calves, or with young unborn, the females being broader across the body and slower in movement, as well as yielding more oil, are more easily captured than the males.
This and the fact that whales are hunted at all seasons, should induce the authorities to adopt reasonable restrictive measures for the preservation of these valuable creatures. The indiscriminate slaughter of whales in the North sea, the Atlantic, and Gulf of St. Lawrence, has practically destroyed the industry in those waters, and without protection the same thing is likely to occur on this coast.
I am informed by men who live on the coast that the practice prevails of capturing the young calf whale, harpooning and anchoring it at the shore, and waiting till the mother whale comes up, seeking its release, when both are slaughtered together. I say that is a practice absolutely inhuman and should not be tolerated in a civilized country. If this whaling industry is going

to last for any time it must be conserved. I am told that the profits from whaling amounts to from twenty to forty per cent. Now it can easily be seen that in consequence of such methods the whaling industry in a few years will be totally extinct. I trust the present government will take these things into consideration, and if it be necessary to do so, take the question up with other nations who are interested, and see that the whaling industry on the Northern Pacific coast is adequately protected, and that such inhuman and unreasonable methods of fishing, as I have described, should be put a stop to. From every standpoint the fishing industry is one that the government should endeavour to conserve, both from the standpoint of revenue, and the standpoint of building up a population on the Pacific coast which will constitute a bulwark for the Dominion of Canada. For the prairie provinces it is essential that they should have a port on the Pacific coast, if their development is going to be what they hope it will be. If the Pacific coast is going to be of any use to Canada then it must be under the direct control and dominance of our own countrymen, people of our own race and sentiment, of our own religion, morals and national ideas. I do not think that we should any longer permit the present condition to obtain, and continue to issue licenses to Japanese and Chinese, thereby fostering a policy which has already proved most suicidal to the fisheries. It is necessary for our future welfare that we build up on the Pacific coast a population which will be a credit to Canada, and a bulwark to this Dominion; and permit me to say in conclusion, that I think the time is not far distant when the Dominion and the empire will need a bulwark on the Pacific coast.

subtopic: FISHERY PROTECTION SERVICE ON PACIFIC COAST.
speechtext: 1 have no hesitation in endorsing every word that has been uttered by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard). They laid great stress upon the fact of the inadequate patrol of the fisheries on the Pacific coast. I am credibly informed that when the present patrol is out of sight, on the south and west coasts of Vancouver island, which is partly in my constituency, no less than from 200 to 300 vessels of various descriptions are waiting to enter the protected zone and to poach in our Canadian fisheries. I am pleased to hear that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has consented to a very substantial appropriation for the establishment of an efficient patrol service for the protection of our fisheries. I might also acid that it would serve a veiy good purpose on the west coast of Vancouver Island, which is known probably as the most disastrous locality to the mer-79

cantile marine on the Pacific coast, and which has become known as the graveyard of the mercantile business-I say that an efficient patrol service might well be used as an aid to the present life-saving service. My friends and colleagues from British Columbia have pretty well covered the ground, but there is one thing I would like to draw attention of hon. members to. It is not the salmon fisheries or the larger fisheries in which I am particularly interested, but it is the herring fishery. The town of Nanaimo my heme town is the home of the herring industry, and I regret to say that this industry is entirely in the hands of Japanese fishermen. I want also, to criticise the method of issuing licenses which has been heretofore in vogue for herring fisheries, and which has been much abused. 1 am credibly informed, although this is a hard matter to prove, that licenses given to wfiite people have been farmed out to Japanese fishermen for a consideration, ranging all the way from $750 to $1,500. As I say, this is difficult to prove, but it is generally believed to be a fact. It is an easy matter for the white man who has got a license to establish, at least ostensibly a half interest or otherwise with Japanese fishermen. After the 21st of September last when I was elected to represent the constituency of Nanaimo, I was requested to thoroughly investigate the question of issuing licenses for the herring fisheries. I did so in conjunction with the local inspector, and we made a thorough investigation into the method of issuing licenses. The result of that investigation was to convince me that the process at present in vogue has resulted in a great number of these licenses being transferred from white ifien to Japanese in ar: illicit manner, and consequently I recommended that these licenses should be refused to other than bona fide operators which has accordingly been done. I hope the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who has this matter in hand will carefully look into the matter and see that this scandal with regard to the issuing of fishery licenses is removed. I am of the opinion which has been expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements), that these fishery licenses should be given to the actual fishermen themselves and only to them. Fish is the people's food and should be as free as the air. At present the licenses fall into the hands of corporations and combinations of capitalists, so that the poor fishermen stand but a slim chance of gaining a livelihood out of the fishing industry. I believe it is contrary to the British fishery-law to refuse a license to any applicant offering to pay the :fee. I will quote a few words from 'the British Fishery Act of 1865, which I do not think has been since amended in. any . way so as to alter the principle laid down.

All persons demanding to purchase licenses, and tendering to any person appointed bv the hoard to distribute the same the amount of license duty to be paid under the provisions of this Act, shall he entitled to receive the same without any question or objection whatsoever.
Now, is there any reason why such a permit or license should be withheld from our fishermen on the Pacific coast, ot anywhere else? Reverting to the question of the patrol, some of my colleagues from British Columbia have dwelt more particularly upon the need of better prevention against poaching in our waters. But we have another patrol, which is the inside patrol, whose duty it is to deal with the offenders against the stipulations of the Fishery Act. In my town of Nanaimo there is stationed the patrol ' Alcedo,' which has a speed of about 8 knots an hour, while every Japanese fishing launch in that harbour has a greater speed, and every one of those launches is fitted up with powerful searchlights. One of these launches always remains constantly in sight of the 'A'lcedo/ and when the 'Alcedo ' gets up steam for the purpose of going out to patrol the fisheries, by a system of telegraphy and signals the news is flashed to every other launch in the vicinity. It follows, consequently, that as the government patrol is a slow boat, comparatively, she is unable to overtake the illicit poaching vessels. I believe that the government patrol vessels should be obliged to carry a searchlight, but in point of fact she has none; and when we referred the matter to the proper authorities we were simply told that a searchlight was not necessary. I think that not only is a searchlight necessary, but that the patrol, both inside and outside, should be of such speed that no other fishing vessel should be allowed to get away, and evade the law in this manner. With regard to persons to whom the licenses should issue, I am of opinion that every man who pulls an oar should be granted a license, and Should have an opportunity of deposing of his fish in the best market and at the best obtainable price. Now the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) put a question to the hon. member from Comox-Atlin, and while I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, if it is permissible for one member to answer a question put to another member, I would assure the hon. member from Guysborough that as far as I am concerned I would have no hesitation whatever in stating that I certainly would eliminate the Orientals from the fishing industry. Now the question of naturalizing the Japanese into British subjects and giving them the rights of citizenship will doubtless present some difficulties, if we are going to eliminate them from the fishing industry. However, I go so far as to say that not only in the fishing industry, Mr. SHEPHERD
but in every other industry of British Columbia where the Japanese or other Orientals enter into competition with our own workers, and notwithstanding anything in international law or international agreement, it is manifestly unfair to allow these Orientals to enter into competition with our white men.
Now, Mr. Speaker, permit me to say a word or two with regard to the Oriental question.
There is no quid pro quo. Our own people cannot engage in the fisheries or enter into any other industry in Japan or India. Therefore, the advantage is clearly on the side of the Asiatic and the present system is manifestly unfair to our own workers. I sincerely trust that the members of this House, will, without regard to party politics, endeavour to frame laws for this country such as will eventually tend to a white Canada. I do not know that I have anything further to say. The Oriental question will probably come up before this House at an early date and I shall then have more to say on the subject, but in the meantime I am thoroughly in accord with the sentiments which have been expressed here this afternoon. I trust that hon. members on both sides of this House will give us their support in our endeavour to eliminate some of the disadvantages under which our people are labouring on the Pacific coast.

Mr. Speaker, this is a question in which I am very much interested. I represent a territory adjoining the riding which is represented by my hon. friend from Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements), and we derive our fish from the waters that lave the shores of northern British Columbia. I am informed by men who are competent to give an opinion that there are to-day in Hecate straits the most valuable halibut fisheries not only in Canada, but in the world, and if that is so-and I believe it is so-we have there a perennial asset which, it strikes me, it would be well for us as Canadians to conserve. The evidence which has been presented here this afternoon by gentlemen who represent constituencies in British Columbia is to the effect that American fishermen are invading our northern waters and taking the fish which are rightfully ours. Up to the present time we have not protected the fisheries in British Columbia. The fisheries of our country form an asset which, I think, has never been properly valued and the fisheries of the Pacific coast have not been properly investigated or protected. That is shown by the fact that the size of the halibut has been reduced from 100 pounds to 20 pounds as was mentioned by one hon. gentleman who spoke this afternoon. That is a strik-

ing fact. If, in the few years which have elapsed since the fisheries in British Columbia began to be exploited, the size of the halibut has decreased from 100 pounds, it is a striking illustration of how these fisheries are being depleted. We are building the Transcontinental railway which has its Pacific terminals at Prince Rupert and nearly opposite are the valuable fishing grounds of Hecate straits. There are today fish companies who are putting in large investments of capital to care for the fish which shall eventually be taken in Hecate straits and transported to western Canada. We have west of here the prairie provinces which are being populated at a very rapid rate. Those provinces have practically no fisheries of their own except those of their lakes and rivers. The result is that in a very few years we are going to have a vast fish market in Canada, and in those prairie provinces particularly, and we have beyond the range of mountains on the Pacific coast the greatest halibut fisheries to be found anywhere. It is a matter that calls for the consideration of this parliament and the consideration of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) in order to see that these valuable fisheries are conserved. What about the fisheries that surround the coasts of the British Isles? These fisheries have existed since the time the Romans invaded Britain and they are still one of the greatest assets of the British Isles because there they pay particular attention to the conservation of that great national asset. Some one mentioned here this afternoon the value of training on our maritime province coasts men who can man a merchant marine. There is no doubt in my mind that the time is not far distant when we shall have again a great merchant marine not only in the maritime provinces, as we had in years gone by, but also on the Pacific coast as well. It is an important factor in the development of the country, particularly a country like ours which has a line of sea-coast on the Atlantic as well as the Pacific, that we should have men who are capable of manning such a merchant marine as I think we may reasonably hope to have in a few years. The merchant marine upon the Pacific coast has not, up to the present time, been as important a factor as we would like to have had it, but time will change that. I am glad to know that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has placed a sum in the estimates sufficient to cover the purchase of boats to protect the great fisheries like those of Hecate straits and other parts of the British Columbia coast and which represent such a great national asset.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The House must have listened with pleasure and profit to the discussion we have had in regard to fishery matters in the province of British Columbia, and I believe the hon. member for Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements) and the other gentlemen from British Columbia who have spoken in reference to this question, are entitled to the thanks of the House for the very great amount of information they have given us concerning these British Columbia fisheries. I would point out to my hon. friend from Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements), that the motion as made would call for all letters written by Captain Newcombe upon the subject of the movements of the ship, and crew, and for a'll formal letters, and such a motion would cover a vast amount of correspondence. I presume that my hon. friend does not want all the papers that would be included in the scope of such a motion, and I would suggest that he let me know just what the papers are that he desires to have brought before the House, in order that there may be a time limit fixed, and then there would be no difficulty whatever in giving to my hon. friend at an early date the information he desires. I may say that the information the department has in its possession with regard to the fishery protection service in British Columbia waters is entirely in agreement with the views expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Atlin (Mr. Clements) and other hon. gentlemen from British Columbia. There is no doubt at all that the fisheries of British Columbia are a very great national .asset. The fishing industry is a growing industry on the Pacific coast, and the fisheries of that province are increasing not only along the shores' of the mainland and the adjoining islands, but also on both shores of the Queen Charlotte Islands, and on the west coast of the Island of Vancouver. There is no doubt whatever but that if these fisheries are carefully preserved and wise laws enacted to that end, and these laws fairly enforced, that the fisheries of British Columbia will be an increasing source of wealth to the country for very many years to come. From biblical times down to the present, fish has largely been the food of the people whose purses are not so large or so long as those of the wealthy classes. I think the universal opinion of this House would be that moneys expended for the purpose of protecting fisheries, and increasing them as a national asset by stocking with fish streams, and lakes and rivers that have been depleted, by unwise conduct in the past, would be well spent in the interests of the country. I am sure this House would not begrudge making appropriations of a

generous character for that work. There is no doubt whatever that the money so expended, if wisely spent, will be returned to the people of Canada many times oyer in the increased wealth of their fisheries. I have said that the information which the department has at its disposal with regard to the protection of the fisheries in British Columbia agrees very largely indeed with the views which hon. gentlemen have expressed in this House this afternoon. The belief of the department is that the protection afforded to our fisheries, by the fishery protection service, within the three mile limit has been inadequate and inefficient. I may say in this connection that I do not think that the statement made to-day by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Shepherd) as to the tremendous amount of poaching that goes on within the three mile limit in the waters contiguous to British Columbia, is at all exaggerated or overdrawn. It might seem at first thought, that the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Shepherd), that sometimes several hundred vessels come within the three mile limit for the purpose of poaching on the wealth that belongs to the Dominion of Canada, was to some extent overdrawn. But the information received from official reports, and from the officers of the department, as well as from the members who represent British Columbia constituencies, and others who are interested in the fisheries there, would lead me to the conclusion that these statements have not been exaggerated in the least. It is my belief that up to the present time there has not been adequate protection to preserve these fisheries from the encroachments of those who have no right to fish in our waters within the three mile limit. It is my belief, also, that there has not been a sufficient patrol to enforce our laws within that three mile limit. Bearing that in mind, I would ask my hon. friends to look at the estimates submitted to the House for the present year and there they will see that provision is made for the better protection of the British Columbia fisheries. There is a vote taken in these estimates for two more vessels to he added to the protection fleet and also provision is be ing made for another vessel for the purpose of patrolling the waters. Criticism has been made to-day by one hon. gentleman on the fact that the Fishery Protection Service is at present under the control of the Naval Service Department, and it was said that it would be more effective if it were placed under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I have noticed a similar contention set up in a resolution which has been sent to me from a meeting of the Fishermens' Association of the county of Charlotte, New Brunswick, a county which has most extensive Mr. HAZEN.
fisheries, in which are situated the islands of Grand Manan, Campobello, Deer Island and others, the population of which chiefly derive their living from the seas, Well, I am not very much impressed with the force of that argument. It must he remembered that the Naval Service Department is as much under the control of the Minister of the Marine and Fisheries De-parment as is the Marine and Fisheries branch itself, and I do not see how the service would be any better enforced under the one branch than under the other.
Every day the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is in consultation with the Deputy-Head of the Naval Service, and there is no reason in the world why the fishery protection service should not be just as well administered where it now is, as if it were transferred to the Marine and Fisheries branch. Probably, one reason which caused the late government to place the fishery protection under the Department of Naval Affairs, is, that in a certain sense the fishery protection fleet is a militant fleet. It exists for the purpose of keeping poachers, chiefly our American friends, from coming into the waters of Canada, and therefore it would seem fitting that it should be under the naval service department. I may say that the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service is a gentleman who was previously deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and consequently he is thoroughly conversant with ail matters affecting fishery protection, and I believe he is rendering excellent service in administering the affairs of the department subject to the control of the minister who is responsible to this House. In the estimates of this year there is an appropriation of $275,000 for additional vessels for the fishery protection fleet of British Columbia. It is hoped that with this money we will be able to purchase a vessel that will be able to go into commission at a very early date so as to be effective this year. Heretofore the protection cruisers employed in the waters of British Columbia have not been suited for the purpose. They were too slow, they were not able to move about quickly from one place to another in order to drive off the American poachers who, tempted by the wealth of our fisheries, paid no regard to our laws. It is to be hoped that with this vote we will be able to get two effective vessels to protect our fisheries and to drive off those who come within our waters to poach on the heritage of Canadians in those fisher-ics.
The service in the past has been performed by the Canadian government steamer the 'Kestrel', with the assistance of sonm smaller vessels. The steamer ' Kestrel " never will be fitted for the service, has been dismantled, and will shortly be sold. 1 Negotiations are now proceeding for the
IMS!)

purchase of a suitable vessel, and in addition it is proposed to ask for tenders at a very early date, as soon as the necessary funds are placed at our disposal by parliament, for the construction of a vessel which in point of size, speed equipment and everything else, will be well suited for the protection of our fisheries on the Pacific coast. One of the hon. gentlemen who addressed the House this afternoon expressed the hope that that vessel would be built in British Columbia. I sincerely hope that will be the case. It will largely depend on the tenders we receive from British Columbia. The tenders are open to all; hut I agree with my hon. friend that it is well for us to have work of this kind performed by Canadian mechanics, so that the money will be spent among our people, provided the percentage of cost above the cost on the other side of the Atlantic is not too great to justify us in taking that course. That will have to be determined when the tenders are received.
I hope that the result of those tenders will be that we can fairlj and properly, having regard to the interests of Canada, have the vessel built in British Columbia, where its work will be, and where I believe people should be able to construct vessels on as favourable terms and conditions as in any other part of Canada. In the meantime, before that other vessel is constructed, something will have to be done for the protection of the fisheries, and an item of $50,000 will be found in the estimates submitted to the House by the Naval Department this year, for vessels to patrol the Pacific coast. It is intended to charter two whaling steamers to do the patrol work on the Pacific coast. These vessels it is calculated can be got at $100 a day, pending the construction of new vessels for the service. I trust that when these vessels are obtained and in Icommission, there will be very much less complaint about vessels from the United States and other countries coming and poaching in our waters and taking the fish which belong to the Canadian people. In addition to that, there is in the estimates of the Fisheries Department this year an item of $75,000 for the purpose of providing the cost of building a fisheries patrol steamer for British Columbia. The difference between the fisheries protection vessels which are under the control of the Naval Department and the fisheries patrol vessels is probably well known to hon. members. The primary object and purpose of the fisheries protection steamers is to protect our waters against smugglers. The object of the fisheries patrol steamers is to enforce the laws and regulations of the department with regard to our fisheries in those waters. In addition to the patrol work, it is absolutely necessary that the inspectors should have a boat which can go along the coast
at a fair rate of speed and practically in all weathers, as there are no railways along the shore and no means of communication except what is afforded by vessels of this sort. The fisheries of the province are rapidly extending, not only along the main shore and the islands contiguous thereto, but as I said before both sides of the Queen Charlotte Islands and on the west ccast of Vancouver Island. It is necessary to protect this great wealth, which will be much greater in the future, and therefore these vessels should be provided. When these plans are carried out, I think we shall have an effective protective service, and if it is not perfectly effective, I shall not hesitate to ask parliament for further provision to enable us adequately to protect the fisheries in the province of British Columbia.
My hon. friends from British Columbia this afternoon dealt with some other matters outside of the four corners of the resolution submitted to the House by my hon. friend from Comox-Atlin. There was a very general interesting discussion with regard to the fishery conditions that exist in British Columbia. While I do not want to draw general conclusions from insufficient data, and while my knowledge and experience of the department are as yet of such a character that I cannot speak with the authority that I would like, I believe there is reason for the very strong criticism indulged in by my hon. friends from British Columbia with regard to the fishery laws and regulations generally in that province. There was some discussion with regard to the issue of licenses. These licenses are issued by the department, and at $25 each. The British Columbian government exacts a license fee of a similar amount; and, according to the records of the department and the information I have obtained from the officials, it has been the habit in the past to grant these licenses to many people who are not fishermen and who are not connected with the fisheries on the Pacific coast. In some cases they have been granted to men engaged in mercantile life, sometimes to clerks in mercantile! establishments. These men have obtained the licenses, not with the intention of embarking in fishing enterprises themselves, but for the purpose of selling them to those who did. In some cases licenses obtained from the government in this way for $25 have been sold for as high as $1,500. This year up to the present time no licenses have been issued. This is a matter which is engaging the attention of the department. The fishery officeis or the department in British Columbia have been instructed not to issue licenses to the persons who obtains them last year, and who did not bma fide engage in the fishing indus-

try. The whole question of these licenses is under consideration. I have had audiences cn the subject with gentlemen from British Columbia, I have consulted the British Columbia government, and I have summoned here the inspector of British Columbia, so that there will be a full discussion of the whole matter with the view, if possible, of remedying the conditions which have been the subject of so much complaint for years. It seems to me indefensible that persons should be able to obtain a license for $25, and sell it again for a large sum of money without rendering any service therefor. Iff these licenses are worth these large sums of money, it is fair to consider whether we should not so arrange the issue of them that these large sums should come into the coffers of the Dominion, and not go into the pockets of private individuals who have rendered no value for them.
In New Brunswick, where we have valuable inland fisheries-salmon and trout fisheries suitable for angling-the practice is to lease them for periods of ten years, the lease being put up to auction, and granted to the highest bidders. Whether that be practicable in connection with the British Columbia fisheries, I am not prepared to say; but it is worth considering whether the country . could not derive greater benefit from those extensive salmon, herring and other fisheries than by granting licenses at nominal prices to persons who simply get those licenses for the purpose of selling them out to others. There is one condition in connection with those British Columbia fisheries, which caused me a great deal of surprise and made me doubt whether hon. gentlemen opposite c'ou'ld have been aware of its existence. From the little study I have been able to give the subject, it seems to me that the fisheries of British Columbia have been administered in the interest of the can-ners and their establishments rather than that of the fishermen. While the canners have been protected by regulations in every possible way, the fishermen have been 'left to their own resources. In fact they have been absolutely hampered in their business. Every cannery has a certain number of licenses issued in connection with it. There is what is called a boat rating for every *cannery. One cannery, for instance, is allowed 200 fishing boats, another 100, and so on, according to the size of the establishment, and outside of those licenses the fishermen are not allowed to pursue their calling. The canneries form practically a close corporation, and the regulations have been framed in the past for the protection of the canners and not at all in the interests of the fishermen. The other day there was brought to my attention a most extraordinary regulation. Under it the fishermen were absolutely prohibited from send-Mr. HAZEN.
ing their fresh fish out of the country. They had to have their fish canned or smoked or they could not sell them outside the province. The effect of that regulation was this. A boat might catch 300 or 400 salmon, and on bringing its catch to the cannery would find a notice posted up to the effect that on that day the cannery would not take more than 100. One would think that the fisherman then could take his fish either, to the American or some other market, No, under the regulation he was absolutely prohibited from doing so, so that he had to dump his extra supply-in some cases 200 or 300 salmon-back into the sea. Thus the catch was entirely lost to him, and no one else got any advantage from it. Under the law he had no right to throw his dead salmon back into the sea, but that was the easiest way of- getting rid of them. Nor was he allowed to use them on land for the purpose of fertilizing. Were the law strictly enforced, all he could do would be to dig .a hole in the ground and there bury his fish. Acting on the representations of representatives from British Columbia, endorsed by the officials of my department, on Saturday last I had that regulation repealed so that now the fishermen can send their fresh fish to other markets than to the canneries. The regulation we have repealed was probably passed years ago, before the fisheries were properly understood and when probably some wealthy men had sufficient influence to have this regulation made in their own interest. It was then continued in force from year to year until it became a serious scandal, and a great subject of grievance to the fishermen.
It is very desirable that the question of our fisheries should be fully discussed in this House. It is very desirable from the standpoint of the general public and also from that of the minister who is the responsible head of the department concerned, and also because such discussion cannot fail to attract attention to the fisheries of British Columbia and other parts of our country.
With reference to the whale fisheries, to which one hon. member from British Columbia has referred, that is a question which can only be dealt with by international arrangement. Whales are caught outside of the three mile limit-outside of waters which are within the territorial jurisdiction of Canada-and, therefore, any regulation for the preservation of those fisheries will have to be a matter of arrangement between the United States and Canada. In a report submitted a short time ago by Captain Bernier of the 'Arctic', he drew attention to the fact that these fish in the northern waters were becoming exterminated and would soon become a thing of the past if regulations were not made to prohibit the fishing and the selling of them for a number of years. I talked the mat-

ter over with the officials of my department and instructed them to take proper steps for the purpose of endeavouring to have an international arrangement come to with the United States and thus prevent valuable fisheries from becoming entirely destroyed.
I assure the House that the desire of the Marine and Fisheries Department is to afford as adequate protection as possible to the very valuable fisheries we possess in British Columbia, so that that great source of supply may not only be continued for years to come, but that the catch may be increased under such wise regulations as may commend themselves, to our approval. The papers called for will be laid on the table, and I shall be happy at any time to discuss this interesting question with any of the representatives from British Columbia.

I have listened this afternoon with great interest to the discussion regarding the fisheries on our Pacific coast. But two questions were raised by hon. members from British Columbia without drawing any comment from the hon. minister. Yet these questions have been discussed in thart province for a number of years, and I understood were issues there in the recent election. The first one is the abolition of Oriental labour in connection with the prosecution of fisheries on the Pacific coast. That question was raised by a number of hon. gentlemen this afternoon, and the (minister will remember that the prohibition of Oriental labour was advocated by them very strongly. The second question is the abolition of the (bonding privilege which enables American fishing vessels to catch fish on the Pacific coast and enables the Canadian Pacific railway to carry that catch free of duty to the Boston market. The abolition of that bonding privilege also was advocated by supporters of this government during the recent election in the Pacific province and was strongly urged this afternoon. But I have not heard the hon. minister say what the policy of the government is on these two important questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I did not refer to what was said regarding the fishing by Japanese in the waters of British Columbia as I did not wish to do so until I had studied the question further, and felt I could speak on it with more authority than at present. The question is in a large measure an entirely new one to me. It is very important and far reaching, involving not only domestic and local conritions, but to some extent our international relations as well, and until I have had more time to study it, I would not feel warranted in giving expression to any decided opinion.
With reference to the bonding privilege, that is worthy of most careful consideration. It is a question that will be considered by the government in the very near future.	.
Everything relating to that very important asset, our fisheries on the Pacific coast, will have the most careful study at the hands of the goverhment. The matter is one outside of party politics altogether, but none the less of great importance to the province of British Columbia and the other provinces as well, and I can assure the House that it will have at my hands the most serious consideration. He said:	Mr. Speaker, the question of
the extension of branch lines of the Intercolonial Railway in Nova Scotia, has been brought before this House from time to time during the last 30 years. The result of the agitation carried on by members on both sides of politics has been an extension of only 90 miles of railway in Cape Breton. I need not point out that it is impossible to serve that country which is 125 or 150 miles long by from 80 to 90 miles wide with a straight single line of railway. It may be that the Minister of Railways and other members of the government do not understand that the Island of Cape Breton is practically two islands. It is cut in two by that magnificent body of salt water the Bras D'Or lakes, from the mouth of the Big Bras D'or to the St. Peter canal, at which point the two sections of the island are connected by a narrow isthmus of half a mile which is cut through by the St. Peter's canal. You have two large areas of land, one to the north and one to the south of the canal and a large salt water lake, in some places 25 miles wide, dividing them. The immense task has been attempted of serving these two bodies _ of land by one railway. The best possible course was adopted when that line of railway was run down through the centre crossing at the Grand Narrows, which is_ approached by a very substantial steel bridge, thus avoiding a ferry at that point. But we can never have a satisfactory or suitable service until there is a railway running through the northern island, and also through the southern end. We are glad to know that a desirable route on the southern side of St. Peter's has been surveyed, and if the road is extended as we

hope it will be extended, down through Locih Lomond toy Mira Valley and through to Lewisburg, that magnificent section of country will be served. Until that is done, that section will not get a proper service. We hear a great deal from hon. gentlemen from British Columbia, who put before this House the necessity and the great demand of their great province.
When I witness the zeal and determination with which those gentlemen present to this House the interests of their great province, I feel that we from the eastern part of Canada are far too timid, far too easily put off, and that we do not put the interest of the people of that part of the country before the House with that force of determination which are characteristic of our friends from the west, and from the province of British Columbia. We are proud to hear of the wealth of the fisheries in British Columbia. I come from the province of Nova Scotia, where we have a wealth of fisheries just as great, perhaps not as great in salmon, but a greater variety and better quality than they have even in British Columbia; and if it is necessary that they should have proper facilities to develop their fisheries, it is equally necessary that rye should have them in the province of Nova Scotia. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say a few days ago that his government intended giving facilities to the fisheries of Nova Scotia such as they never had before. Let me tell the Prime Minister that it is impossible for him to give us the proper means to develop the fisheries in Nova Scotia until he puts the great fishing points in touch with railway communication.^ It is unnecessary for me to tell the Prime Minister and the government that every year and every day the fresh fish of the Dominion are becoming more important, and any part of Canada that cannot compete in that great industry with regard to fresh fish is not in the race. It is the opinion of the best men in Nova Scotia engaged in the fishery that we cannot compete in the market until we are, from Yarmouth to Scattaree, put in touch with railway lines, and until the Department of Railways puts upon the Intercolonial and its branches refrigerator cars capable of catering to this trade. While we are dependent for the carrying of our fresh fish on freight trains and insufficiently equipped freight cars we are not in the race with other parts of the country and other parts of the continent who are looking after this trade. Now it is impossible for the government to develop this fish business until we have facilities with which to develop it. We have all along the coast of Nova Scotia from Yarmouth to Scattaree, and from Scattarep to Cane North, and all around

But at this time of the year when the ice comes in, and they cannot send their fish away by water they are completely shut out from the world. The only thing that will relieve the situation is the extension of this line of railway that I am now advocating .to Baddeck, and then the opportunity will present itself to extend it north along the harbours of St. Ann, Ingonish, and Neil's Harbour, clean to the Bay of St. Lawrence to Meat Cove, skirting along the most magnificent fishing grounds in Canada, and giving the people of this country an opportunity of competing in the markets of the world with their codfish, their salmon, their haddock, their herring, and a hundred and one kinds of magnificent edible fish caught in these waters. That has been the situation for the'last 150 years. And when, from time to time, ever since there was a parliament in Canada, the members from that part of the country coming here have always been advocating the expenditure of this pittance of money necessary for extending the railway, is it surprising that we should persist from time to time in keeping at it until the government will see to it that the interests of the people are met as they should be? I am not talking railways, because I am in opposition.
I was talking railways when I was not in opposition. I am making the same I speeches, putting forward the same argu-! ments now that I was putting forward in

the local House when I was there ten; years ago. This is my third parliament here, and I have been every session talking the same things before this House. So it cannot be said that 1 am talking in opposition in a way that I would not be talking if I were a supporter of the government. Last year I was told that at last we had reached the point where the good people of the county of Victoria, and of the island of Cape Breton generally were to receive that which was their due; a sum of $200,000, which would be a fair amount to start with, was put in the estimates. Of that sum five-twelfths were passed before prorogation, and since we came back here the other seven-twelfths have been passed by this government, adopting apparently the policy of the outgoing government. There was no criticism from either side that the amount was more than necessary to make a fair start on this railway.
