Mir. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Portage la Prairie) moved second reading of Bill (No. 7), to amend the Railway Act. He said: I presume that the remarks of the right hon. gentleman in reference to the Bill of my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff), will have application to the Bill which I now move the second reading of. I appreciate the position taken by the right hon. gentleman, that in view of the purpose to immediately consolidate the Railway Act it would be well not to pass, at present, any legislation of this character. There is, however, a situation obtaining in the country to-day with regard to one feature of our railway legislation, to which the attention of parliament ought to be emphatically drawn, and I trust that when the government comes to consolidate the Railway Act it will introduce into it provisions along the lines laid down in this Bill. It will be observed at once that this legislation touches ground that has been fought over time and again in parliament, and that, I may say, has been battled upon for fifty years in the courts of Canada. It touches the question of the liability of railway companies for the loss caused by the killing or injuring of animals by their trains or engines. Legislation with respect to this matter was passed in 1903 at the instance of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) and, as I understand it, that hon. gentleman is in gre'at part, if not altogether, responsible for the present wording of sub-section 4 of section 294 of the Railway Act. It is this subsection which in one of its features the Bill purposes to alter in order to meet the conditions which prevail almost wholly I believe in western Canada. This Bill purposes to amend the present state of affairs by a method which has two features. The first is, by endeavouring to fix upon a standard cattle guard which shall be of real use for the purpose for which it is intended. It provides, by amending the subsection I have referred to, in cases where animals are injured on the tracks of a railway company and where the injury is caused by the negligence of the company, that the company shall be made to pay. In introducing this legislation I am not moved by any desire to cater to any unwarranted public feeling against railway corporations. I am one of those who believe that a corporation, however large, is entitled to the full benefit of just laws. But, I believe, that, whether by an error of parliament or not, the Railway Act at present is such that the owners of animals are placed at a serious disadvantage in con-

tending for their rights in the courts, a disadvantage which they would not suffer if even the common law prevailed. It will be necessary for me, in order to make clear the necessity for this amendment, to state what the present law is, and I shall endeavour to do so concisely and with the use of as few technical terms as possible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman now dealing with both his proposed amendments?
To the first amendment I do not attach anything like the importance I do to the second, in clause 2 of the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In order to make it perfectly plain will the hon. gentleman in each case give the' existing legislation, if he has it before him, so that it may be on ' Hansard.'

The first clause of the Bill provides that all cattle guards, to be constructed hereafter, indeed all cattle guards to be used hereafter, shall, as to their method of construction, style, and dimensions, be submitted to the Railway Commission and be approved by them. The existing law in this respect is in section 254 which provides that all fences, gates and cattle guards to be erected by railway companies shall be such as are suitable and sufficient to protect cattle or other animals getting upon the railway lands. It is hard to conceive of legislation more strict in terms than that, it puts upon the railway company the burden of having fences, gates and cattle guards suitable and sufficient to prevent animals getting on the tracks, and in that regard it is hard to improve upon the existing law.
The only addition I make to that is this. I have a clause providing that the cattle guards, which of all appliances of the railway company have proved most effective, be submitted to the Railway Commission, and be approved of by them before they shall be considered sufficient. It may be argued that if we do that, and if the Railway Commission approve of a certain form and size of cattle guard, should animals get over it the railway company might be relieved of liability. I am not prepared to say that will or will not happen; but I do think that if a railway company would provide the very best appliance in this regard, as it would be compelled to do if the commission had to approve of it, there would be much less injury and loss suffered than there is at the present time, when the railway company is compelled to provide no special kind of cattle guard, but just such as is sufficient. So that I think that a substantial reform without any serious risk would be effected if we compelled the companies to submit their cattle guards to the
Railway Commission for approval. But I attach no such importance to section 1 as I do to section 2 of this Bill, because I believe that section 2 will effect the reform that section 1 is intended to assist in effecting. That is to say, section 2, in conjunction with the present law in this regard, will have the effect of making the companies pay where they ought to pay, and if they do, they will see to it that the cattle guard is suitable and sufficient. So that clause 2 is the vital clause of this Bill, and on it I desire to found the brief argument which I intend to present. Section 2 provides that subsection 4 of section 294 of the present Act shall read in this way:
When any horses, sheep, swine or other cattle at large, whether upon the highway or not, get upon the property of the company, and by reason thereof damage is caused to or by such animal, the party suffering such damage shall, except in the cases otherwise provided for by the next following section, be entitled to recover the amount of such damage against the company in any action in any court of competent jurisdiction, unless the company establishes that such animal so got upon the property of the company, without the negligence of the company or the omission of any duty binding on the company under this Act.
Subsection 4 of section 294 is the section of the Railway Act which deals with the case of injury to or by animals when they get on a right of way after being at -large. It has no reference, whatever, to injuries caused to or by animals at highway crossings, or animals that get upon the right of way from an inclosure where they are not at large. The cases of animals which get on the right of way through being at large constitute the large field of cases in which under the present law the railway company is able to escape. In other cases there is no serious complaint. At present the clause in the Act is the same as clause 2 of this Bill, except that after it states that dam age can be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction, it has the following words :
Unless the company proves that 6Uck animal got at large through the negligence or -wilful act of the owner or his agent or the custodian of such animal or his agent.
So that under the present law the company shoulders the burden prima facie; that is to say, if an animal, after being at large, is killed or injured on the right of way, the company is prima facie liable, but it escapes the moment it shows that the animal got at large in the first place through the negligence or wilful act of the owner. The purpose of the Bill is to keep the burden on the company, but to alter that burden. Instead of permitting the company to prove that the animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act of the owner, it says to the company: prove that

your own skirts are clear; no matter how it got at large, prove that it got on your right of way without any negligence or omission on your part. The present burden which the company has to discharge is so light and so capable of being discharged, that in western Canada the company easily escapes in 90 per cent of all the cases that occur, the great majority of which never go to court at all. Now, in the law at present there is a provison that this does not affect the liability of a man who takes down a railway fence or otherwise interferes with railway property. I have omitted that, but I am quite willing that it should be added to the clause as I propose it. To my mind it will be unnecessary in the law, if amended as I propose, but it appears to some that it is necessary, and I have no objection to adding it.
The question before the House' is- whether the law amended as I propose, will meet the exigencies of present conditions better than the old law. I submit that it will. I am free to admit that conditions are not the same all over Canada. In eastern Canada, where industrial and farming life have reached a more advanced stage than in western Canada, the conditions are quite different. In eastern Canada animals are not found at large nor is there any necessity why they should be at large to anything like the same extent as in the west. I do not think it was ever the intention of parliament to legislate that it would be unlawful for animals to run at large in this country, but the effect of the present law is to go to that extent, for we might just as^ well legislate that it is unlawful for an animal to be at large as to legislate that .if it should get at large by some omission of the owner and get into the right of way, where there is no fence, the owner has no redress should an accident occur. That was the judgment in the ease of Clayton and the Canadian Northern, in which case Chief Justice Howell observed that the effect of the law was to prohibit the running at large of animals anywhere in Canada. Any one who knows anything of the west will understand that such a law would work most serious injury to that part of our country. The conditions there are such that it is essential that animals should be allowed to run at large within certain limits and restrictions. In eastern Canada however, that necessity is not so urgent and in that section the law may have worked fairly well. But in the west, there is a daily_ slaughter of animals by railway companies running up into thousands and thousands of dollars, and 90 per cent, of these cases are due to the negligence of the railway companies. I doubt if there is an hon. member from that western country who will not say that the slaughter of animals there by the railways, through night and day, is one of the chief causes of * Mr. MEIGHEN.
hardship and hard times in individual instances and one that mc>3t persistently reaches the ears of members of parliament. That is one of the complaints which is most earnestly and insistently urged by farmers and ranchers through their organizations, and relief from which they have been seeking from this parliament for years back. I doubt if there is one hon. member from the west who will not say that, within his own personal knowledge, the railway companies, through their negligence, whether wilful or not, have been the cause of determining the weal or woe of many of our settlers. Many a man struggling to lift his head above water has had it pushed down again by the slaughter of his animals by railway trains.
Why is this the case, and how is it going to be remedied? It is the case because the running at large of animals in that country is a commercial and industrial necessity. Under the present law, animals at large are not permitted to go within half a mile of the railway right of way. If they do and are killed at a crossing, the railway company is not responsible, unless the animal is in charge of some responsible person. The amendment I propose does not affect that law in any degree, The farmer who lets his animal run at large and whose animal is killed at a crossing will have to bear the loss. That is a risk which the farmer takes if he lets his animal at large in proximity to a railway. Whether that law be just or unjust, I am not saying, but it is the law, and this amendment which I propose does not interfere with it. The farmer takes the risk if his animal is killed on the highway crossing, but if it is killed on the railway, company's track, the company is responsible. If an animal gets on the right of way, prima facie the railway company is responsible, because if the company had complied with the Act, the animal at large could not have got on its right of way. Therefore should the animal be injured, the burden of proof ought to be on the railway company. 90 per cent, of the animals injured or killed were necessarily turned out at large by the farmers.
What will be the result if the law is amended in this direction? It will mean that if a railway fence is down and an animal gets on the track, if the gate is open, if the cattle guard is defective, or if there is no cattle guard, and as a result an animal is killed, then the railway company will be bound to pay, and I ask who should pay in such a case? What is the common law? What is the law that through a thousand years of British jurisprudence has been established, as what is fair and right between man and man? Where there is negligence and loss results, the party whose negligence is the proximate cause of the loss is made to pay. Is that the case

under the present Railway Act? Things are reversed for the benefit of the company. If, through reckless driving of my automobile, I kill a horse on the highway I have to pay for it, and I cannot say that the farmer was negligent by letting his horse on the highway. Although he may have been negligent, his negligence was not the proximate cause of the loss. Why should that be reversed in the case of a railway? That simple common-sense principle is reversed in the case of the Railway Act. The railway company may neglect the simplest precautions in the construction of their road. In the west they seldom have cattle guards, they are not only'1 negligent, but they are wilfully in default, and by reason of that, animals get on the right of way, and are killed. Whose negligence is the proximate cause? Not that of the farmer,who suffers the loss, his is the further cause; the proximate cause is the negligence of the railway company. This question has been argued in courts of law, the case I am presenting has been argued in Carruthers and the Canadian Pacific railway. The Supreme Court of Canada held that by subsection 4 of section 294, that plain condition of the common law was altered, and no matter how negligent the company were, no matter how flagrantly they had violated the provisions of the Railway Act, they utterly escaped liability for the loss caused proximately by that negligence, by simply showing that these animals were at large through the negligent or wilful act of the owner.

As I construe the present law, and I have followed my hon. friend's argument with great interest, by the amendment of 1910, whenever an accident takes place the conduct of the company is not at all in issue, it may be negligent or not negligent, the only question is whether or not the plaintiff himself was negligent. If the plaintiff is negligent he cannot recover, but if not, even although the company is not in default and has complied with the law, the plaintiff must recover.

I quite agree with .the law -as stated by my right lion, friend, but the law as interpreted has the effect of utterly reversing that plain rule of common law. The law as so interpreted holds that the conduct of the railway company is not in question, even if that conduct or misconduct is the proximate cause of the loss. Under the common law, their conduct would be seriously in question and the company would have to pay if it was the proximate cause of the loss. I need not argue whether or not that is the law as interpreted. Members who are familiar with -the law will know that not only in Carruthers and the Canadian Pacific railway, but in several cases it has
been so interpreted and hon. members will recall that in the case of Clayton and the Canadian Northern railway in 1908, where Chief Justice Howell of the Court of Appeals in Manitoba gave a dissenting judgment, His Lordship argued that all the holdings up to that time in favour of the law as I maintain it should not be, were wrong, but he was overruled by the majority of the court, and in that case as in every other one up to the present it has been held that the railway companies utterly escaped no matter how flagrantly negligent they were or how they violated the provisions of the Act. However, negligent they may be they escape by saying that somebody further back was negligent, and in that way they are enabled by the adjudgment of this parliament to reverse a rule of the common law. I should have said that the Supreme Court held the company liable in Carruthers and the Canadian Pacific railway, but the Supreme Court has held and it has been held in numerous cases that the company escape liability if they can throw on the farmer or owner the burden of having negligently allowed the animal at large.
Is that the way you interpret the statute as it now stands?
I would interpret tire statute as the courts do. I would not pretend to give an opinion that would be of value to the House, but I cannot see how the courts could otherwise interpret the law.

Have the courts laid it down that where an animal is on the property of another, a trespasser, the onus is on the person who owns the property to prove that the animal was not on his property by right but improperly?

Yes, the courts have so interpreted subsection 4. This parliament has proceeded upon the assumption that if an animal is on the right of way of a railway company under our Act, and is injured, prima facie the company is responsible, the idea being that the animal could not be there if the company had complied with the law so that there has never been any question on that point, the burden has been on the company and so they have escaped.

The present statute provides that the company shall be liable unless it can prove that the animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act or omission of the owner or his agent or custodian. Then, as I understand the statute and construe the law, the only question for the -court is not to examine what has been the conduct of the company, but what has been the conduct of the plain-
250?

tiff. If the claimant shows that he has not been negligent the company is liable. It is not open to the company then to say: We have fulfilled all the conditions placed on us by the law. The law says that the company, whether it has fulfilled the conditions of the law or not, is liable and must be so unless it can show that the plaintiff is at fault.
And the onus is on the company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the onus is on the company the statute seems to make a prima facie case against the company, but it discharges the company, according to the argument of my hon. friend, upon proof of something which is not directly connected with the cause of the accident. It makes the company liable without proof of negligence, it then discharges the company by proof of some remote cause which is not directly connected with the destruction of the animal.

The only question is this-perhaps I am not getting to the point the leader of the opposition has said, the courts have held that the company is prima facie liable, but they escaped by proving something not immediately connected with the loss, just as the leader of the government states. Now the only question is this -I am not sure it pertains directly to the issue-if an animal is wilfully turned out by the farmer and then gets on the right of way without any neglect whatever on the part of the company, is the company responsible? That is to say, suppose the company has lived up to the law in every regard, take for example a case where they do not have a fence, where the Railway Commissioners do not compel them to fence, and an animal breaks out and gets upon the right of way, is the company responsible? I know of no case where the company has been held responsible in those circumstances. There was the case in British Columbia, Siegel vs. the Canadian Pacific railway, where the company was relieved, so that the leader of the opposition would not be correct in saying that the company's conduct is not in question. The company's conduct is not in question if they show that the owner of the animal negligently turned the animal out, in that case the company's conduct is not in question. But if, on the contrary, it is shown that the animal broke away, and without any negligence on the part of the owner, then the company's conduct may be in question under Siegel and the Canadian Pacific railway. I hope that the decision in Siegel and the Canadian Pacific railway is not good, though I do not wish to give an opinion different to that court in British Columbia, But what is laid down as undoubtedly the law in the western province is this, that

once the company show the animal got at large by the negligence of the owner, then-conduct is no longer in question. Now how should the law be amended? The proposal is to amend it by asking the company to pay the man who turned the animal out. If the animal is turned out negligently and is killed on the highway the farmer loses; but if it gets on the right of way he is prima facie responsible, and if it is killed there then the burden is on him to show that it got there without any negligence on his part, or in violation of the Railway Act. Surely that is simple, and that is what the law ought to be. If an animal is an extraordinary animal, and gets at large, or is turned at large, and the company, has complied -with the law, and the animal is killed, the company should not pay. But if the company has not complied with the law, then the company's neglect, the company's defeasance, is the immediate and approximate cause of the loss, and they ought to pay in every case. Now to illustrate by particular cases, I have no doubt that hon. members of this House could give illustrations of the escape of the company where they should have paid, and every hon. member, if he thinks over his own case, will see that the reason the company escaped was just the reason I have given, because, in the first place, the animal was at large through the negligence, or even through the wilful act of the owner. I know, for instance, of one case where a man was leading a horse to water and two others were following. Only one was being led by the halter, and there was no fence between him and the highway. Something frightened the animals and they got away, including the one that was being led. There was no fence on the railway to protect the track, they got upon the railway track, two of them were killed, the one that was being led with the halter, and one of those that were following. Now it will be clear to the House where the owner of those animals will land in a court of law. In respect of the one that was being 'led, that one did not get at large through the negligence or wilful act of the owner, very likely the company would be made to pay. In the case of the other one that was not being led, although the company's negligence was the cause of its loss, the only cause of its loss, the immediate and proximate cause, the company escapes. Then take the other case. There have been cases of ranchers in the west, farmers in the west, having animals by the score at large because, in the great majority of cases, there is no fencing at all; it would be practically impossible to carry on business in that country to keep them always within an enclosure. Now, if the railway fences are up, and if the cattle guards are there as provided by

the Act, if the gates are up and closed as provided by the Act, and things are moderately safe, the animal may be killed at a crossing and the man loses, that is all there is about it. He takes that risk when he turns them out. But if the animal, through the negligence of the company, gets upon the right of way through there being no fence in violation of the law, or no "cattle guard in violation of the law, or through there being no gate or a poor gate, or a poorly fastened gate, why should they not pay? The Court of Appeals has held the contrary, and there could be no doubt under their reading of the law. If what my friend behind me says were the law there would be no object in amending it; if it were not held that the company escapes when they prove that the animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act of the owner, there would be no purpose in amending the law. That would be alL right. But the unfortunate thing is that that has not been held to be the law, and it appears to me that it is not intended to be the law by subsection 4 as it at present reads.
Now I wish to make reference to the present condition of the obligation of the company in regard to fencing, to gates and to cattle guards, because I wish to show that at the present time and under present conditions, there might possibly be a very few cases where, under the present law the owner might recover and under the law as amended he might not, there might possibly be cases, though extremely rare, if any at all, and in the course of a short time there could be none.
Now, it is well known that, under the authority of the Railway Act, the Board of Railway commissioners have power to compel railway companies to fence their right of way, or, in other words, the company has to fence its right of way and provide gates and cattle guards unless absolved by the Railway Commission. Under the authority of that Act, the Board of Railway commissioners undertook to make an order that, before the expiration of a certain date, all railway companies in this country should have their fences erected and their cattle guards and gates provided. That was a general order applicable to all railways in Canada and of effect throughout the whole country. From that order the railway companies appealed and, as I understand it, the Supreme Court of Canada held that the board had not power to make so general an order that their orders must be definite and confined to specific areas. In accordance with that ruling of the Supreme Court, the railway commissioners, have, since that time, made very sweeping orders, but none so sweeping as to be ruled ultra vires by the Supreme Court. The policy of the board has been to bring about, at the earliest
possible date, the time when it shall be compulsory all over this country for fences, gates and cattle guards to be provided and that even though the neighbourhood is not fenced and closed or inhabited the company's right of way must be fenced and gates and cattle guards provided. I am informed, if not by the commission, at all events by a member, that it is expected within a year that all the railways of this country will be, under order from the board of railway commissioners, and that a valid order, compelled to have their fences, gates and cattle guards completed. Before the expiration of that time if a case arose where a railway company were not in default, that is where they did not have to erect a fence or cattle guard, and an animal got on the line by tne negligence of the owner and was killed, if under such circumstances it were held by our courts that in the meantime under the present law the company would have to pay, they would no.t have to pay under this amendment. I do not say it \frould be so held, but I do say that the number of cases will be practically nil, and that we might just as well consider them a negligible quantity. The great class of cases that comes before the notice of the public, or before the notice of lawyers and the courts, is where the animals are out through the purpose, the designation, the intention of the owner himself and these animals, through the absolute neglect and defiance by the railway company of the law, get upon the right of way and are killed. This represents a great number of cases where injustice is suffered and for which a remedy is urgently needed and demanded. It is that class of cases that this amendment aims at effecting a remedy for and in my humble opinion it certainly effects tbe remedy. In the course of a year, as asserted by the commission, there should be no case where the railway companies could justly be held liable now and would not be held liable under the amended law. So, it seems to me we can be absolutely fair to the companies, make the law clear to them and clear to any man who runs and reads, by passing this legislation and then there will be no case, or very few if any cases at all, where an injustice can be perpetrated. I do not know whether I have made this clear. 1 have endeavoured to put the case as clearly as I could. I make no pretence of having a better knowledge of the law in reference to railways than any other hon. member of this House, and I have the utmost deference for the opinion of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) or any other hon. member who has interrupted me, but I have not come to the House without a thorough investigation in this regard and without actual experience in the courts of law where it has been held, held against me and held on appeal.
[DOT]2511

that the law was just as stated by myself at the present time. I know of cases that occur almost every day, of cases that come-into small offices in the country, week after week, that never get to the courts at all, simply because it is well known and understood that the company can escape by showing that the animal got on the track through the negligence or wilful act of the owner, no matter what their default may be, and it is well known that the company can show this out of the mouth of the plaintiff himself the moment he goes into the box. This will not only alter the ruling of the courts and make it fairer to the farmer, and no more than fair to the railways, but in such cases as have already come to the court it will make the law so clear and plain and the liability so definite and fixed that there will be less litigation than in the past, or, in the great majority of cases, the railway will at once pay. They do at the present time, when they recognize their liability. It is very rarely, speaking comparatively, that they contest a claim in which they are liable at all; they usually pay or make a settlement of some kind, because, by reason of the decisions of the courts, the law has become fairly well known. If the Act is amended along the lines here urged, I believe that eight times for once they pay now, they will pay without any litigation at all, and that not in any case under this law, will they be corn-lie! led, where they have absolute right and justice on their side to pay; that is, wherever they are not responsible, they will not pay. I make no allegation at all that in all respects as affects the railway law in regard to the killing of cattle this goes the whole way in effecting the reform. I say in the case of animals at large which represents the great majority of cases that it goes a long way and effects a great reform.
There will still, perhaps, be a class of cases where loss results and nobody's negligence is the cause, where the railway company is not negligent and therefore not responsible and where the farmer is not negligent and therefore, not responsible. I believe myself that we should move to amend the law in that regard, and, as the Prime Minister stated, the Railway Act is to be amended, I throw out this suggestion, whatever it may be worth, that in that class of cases, where the loss results, and no man's negligence is the cause, namely, the class of cases where the loss results simply from the incidence of the railway companies themselves, that is to say, a loss caused by reason of the operation of a railway, which is a dangerous operation ir>. the country, a loss incident to the running of railway trains, and is founded on the negligence of no person or company at all, I believe that justice would be better met by making the company pay rather Mr. MEIGHEN.
than by making the farmer pay. I do not say that to play the role of demagogue in any way, but I say it after some little consideration and for this reason that while the railway company is a private corporation and a corporation entitled, generally speaking, to just as much protection under the law as a private individual, there is this difference that, especially in later times, a railway company partakes of the nature of a semi-public corporation. There is a great, and increasing sense in which the railway is a corporation of a public character in that its assets become more and more, as the years go by, socially created assets. It is serving a great public rather than a private end and by reason of that fact the gains that a railway-company make, are, or should be, in part, the gains of the public and the losses that a railway company make are the losses of the public.
The gains a railway company makes are the gains of the public, and the losses of a railway company are the losses of the public, and, in the ultimate, the losses suffered by a corporation of this semi-public character fall back upon the public, and that is where losses of the class I have just last referred to should fall. That is to say: losses that are incidental to the operation of railway trains, and that are caused not by the negligence of any one or of any company. It, therefore, would appear to me, as the better legislation, and as the better purpose to be kept in view, to shoulder that class of legislation on the railway corporation instead of leaving it upon the shoulders of the individual. That again is a class of oases not directly affected by this amendment. The purpose to be affected by the amendment I have outlined at the beginning of my remarks, and I urge it upon the attention of the House with all the earnestness of which I am possessed. I believe it will effect an important reform, and that it will effect that reform without doing violence to the duty we owe to corporations, to individuals, or to anybody.

I would like to know if the remedy the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) is seeking for the conditions in the west by this legislation, would apply to the conditions in the province of Nova Scotia. A few years ago in the case of Gordon vs. Dickie, the Supreme Court of Canada held that in Nova Scotia cattle were not permitted to be at large, that the owner was obliged to keep his cattle fenced in, and that if cattle were killed or injured in any way while at large the owner had to bear the loss. The conditions prevailing in the west are similar in some respects to those prevailing in Nova Scotia, where large pastures are held in common, and where the farmers are obliged to allow their cattle to roam at
[DOT]2513

large. As the law at present is, if one of these animals should wander on the right of way, by reason of a defect in the fence, or through a gate being left open negligently by the 'company and the animal is killed, the owner has no recourse. I am heartily in favour of the principle of this Bill as explained by the hon. gentleman. Two years ago, a valuable horse belonging to a constituent of mine, and which was roaming at large, as is the custom in that part of the country, wandered on the Intercolonial through a defect in the feijce which was known to the section foreman for several months, and the animal being killed, application was made to the department for compensation, and the owner was told that, inasmuch as the horse was roaming at large and had not strayed on the right of way from tire owner's property, they were not liable for damages. I should be very glad, indeed, if this principle which the hon. gentleman is seeking to have incorporated in the Railway Act would apply to the Intercolonial as well ns to ev-ery other railway, so that the residents in that part of the country through which the Intercolonial railway runs might get justice in such cases.

Of course, the entire Railway Act applies to the whole of Canada, and the only distinction I drew was that the exigencies of the conditions in western Canada demanded this legislation more than they did elsewhere. The Railway Act is no respecter of provinces, and has the same application to one province as to the other.	-
The decision in Gordon vs Dickie was that cattle were not permitted to be at large in Nova Scotia, and I understand they are so permitted in the west.

In the west, the province delegates to the municipalities the power to allow the running at large of animals, but of course an animal must be kept on the property of the owner, and if it goes beyond that and it is injured the owner is responsible. But that does not affect this Bill. Even though that may be the law, the liability for the death of the animal if it gets on the right of way is altogether another question. I submit that the fact that an animal was killed on the right of way through the negligence of the company should not be a barrier to recovery, and if this Bill should become law it would not be a barrier in Nova Scotia, any more than in the western provinces. As to its application to the Intercolonial railway I do not feel myself qualified to speak.

What the hon. member from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has said as to the importance of this matter might very well give reason for the Prime 80
Minister to change his mind in regard to his decision not to permit any amendments to the Railway Act this session. I can assure the Prime Minister and the government that the condition in the west, because of the legislation as it stands, or, as it is interpreted, is a very great grievance and a very great hardship. It is a condition which has existed for -some time, and I can tell the Prime Minister that the people of the west who are suffering under that grievance cannot look with equanimity upon his decision not to legislate this session in the direction proposed by this Bill. In this case, the right hon. gentleman might very well make an exception, and I think the hon. members representing western constituencies will back up what I say in this regard.
With the amendment itself, as stated in its purpose by the hon. member (Mr. Meighen) I am not altogether in agreement. His complaint against the present law is that the company escapes liability unless the owner of the animal can prove lack of negligence on his part. My fault with this proposal is that the company will under that legislation escape liability unless the claimant can prove negligence on the company's part.
The company has to disprove it.
Theoretically, the company has to disprove it, but in actual practice the claimant would have to prove and the company would thereby, escape.
I do not understand my hon. friend. How could it be in actual practice if it is -not the law.

I will explain. This legislation says that on the company fulfilling certain requirements laid down by the Railway Commission, the company shall not be liable. The Railway Commission cannot lay down a requirement that will be efficient and that the company can fulfil in regard to cattle guards. There is no cattle guard yet invented that will keep cattle off the track. Until such cattle guard is invented it is futile to say that this legislation would protect the owner of the cattle or would lay liability definitely on the railway company beyond the point I have stated.
That is the first section.

The first section read in connection with the second-. The two parts .must be read together; the one affects the other; -and, in my humble judgment, the provision of the first part read in connection with the provisions of the second part "would -absolutely relieve the railway company from- liability. The matter is too serious to be left as- a matter of opinion between my hon. friend and myself. He has stated his reason for -bringing in- the
Bill; I have stated my reasons for disagreeing with the provisions of the Bill as not being effective.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any suggestion?

Yes. Before I make a suggestion, however, I wish to say that the law as it stands at present is, I understand, either entirely or measurably satisfactory to the part of the country where in the ordinary course of affairs all stock is kept in inclosures; bnt just for that very reason it is entirely unsatisfactory to those parts of the country where in the ordinary course of affairs the stock runs at large; and just as soon as the legislation now on the statute-book w>as passed, at that time and always afterwards those parts of the country *where the stock generally speaking runs >at large have felt themselves under a very great disadvantage. This legislation became effective in May, 1910, and during the suimer of 1910 and the summer of 1911 complaint was continually made against the consequences of that legislation. I am not sure who was directly and immediately responsible for that legis-tion, but I am under the impression that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie had something to do with it.
Yes, I introduced the legislation which the government adopted.

There is no doubt of the intent of the legislation, and no doubt of its efficiency in a very large part of the *country; but the very thing that makes it efficient in one part of the country makes it inefficient in another part. I repeat that the condition is so urgent that I think the government would do well to meet the case at this session. As to the suggestion which I have to make, I merely wish to put before the House again the clause of the Bill amending the Railway Act that was introduced at the last session by the late Minister of Railways. That clause was one of a number of clauses amending the Railway Act. It met with such opposition in the House at the time it was brought forwiard that it was dropped out of the Bill in order that the other provisions might go through. But I think that on mature consideration the House will recognize that that provision would be comprehensive and adequate, and would be absolutely fair as between the railway company and the public, while I admit that it does not give the railway company that percentage of advantage which it seems to. have been the principle of all previous legislation to concede. The proposed amendment, which was section 11 of Bill (No. 197) of last session, reads as follows:
Sections 294 and 295 of the principal Act, and sections 8 and 9 of chapter 50 of the statutes Mr. OLIVER.	j ' |
of 1910, are repealed, and the following is enacted as section 294 of the principal Act:- 294. The company shall be liable to the owner for the full value of all horses, sheep, swine or other cattle that may be killed or injured Upon the company's lands through the operation of the railway, save where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person-
(a)	failing to keep the gates at any farm crossing, at each side of the railway closed, when not in use; or,
(b)	leaving open any gate on either side of the railway provided for the use of any farm crossing without some competent person being at or near such gate to prevent animals
issing through such gate on to the railway; or,
(c)	other than an officer, contractor, or
employee of the company, taking down any nart of the railway fence; or,	...
(d)	turning any animal upon or within the enclosure of any railway company; or,
(e)	except as authorized by said Act, with-11* the consent of the company, riding, leading or driving any animal, or suffering it to enter upon any railway and within the fences and guards thereof; or,
(f)	leaving the gates of the company at railway stations open for the convenience of the company.
It will be observed that the principle is laid down in the first section, that if the cattle are killed on the track the company is liable. There is no question about the kind of fence or the kind of cattle guard or whether there is a fence or cattle guard at all. It is up to the company to see that its cattle guard or fence is such as to beep the cattle out, and if the cattle are not kept out, that is all that has to bv shown. Then there must be exceptions to that, and the list of exceptions which I have read practically follows the provisions that are already in the Act. These exceptions^ might be amended or might be added to if that were found necessary; but the main principle is the declaration that if the cattle are killed on the track, the company is liable for their full value. _ That principle I would wish to see embodied in legislation this session, the more so because since May of 1910, as my hon. _ friend from Portage la Prairie has graphically pointed out, the cattle owners of the western country, and, as my bon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has pointed out. the cattle owners in Gape Breton as well, are in practice deprived of the protection of the law as against the railway companies. That is >a condition that should not be allowed to remain for a moment longer than is necessary to pass legislation to cure it.
Last session the then Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) was so convinced of the necessity of remedying the situation that he brought in the legislation which I have already placed before the House. For reasons good or bad that legislation was opposed by my hon. friends from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) Souris,

(Mr. SchafEner) Macdonald, (Mr. Staples) Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster). It is for them to say why. In consequence of their opposition that provision had to be dropped out of the Bill in order that the rest of it might pass. Relief was in sight for the people of the west at that time. That opportunity passed by and another has come, and I am satisfied that the people of that country will feel that their interests are not being properly served unless this opportunity be taken advantage of to meet a very special and urgent condition due more parti cularlv to legislation by this parliament which, while curing a certain evil in one part of the country, left the door open wide to evil in another part.
Does the hon. gentleman not see that the legislation he has just read, takes the burden off the railway companies altogether?
I see quite the contrary.

Does he not remember that when the legislation was before this House the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) moved an amendment making it clear that the burden of proof was on the companies, and the government rejected that amendment.

I do not recall that incident, and I do not know that it is profitable to discuss matters of detail which occurred so long ago; but the point is that this proposal, purports to offer a remedy to an exceedingly undesirable condition. My hon. friend has placed his views before the House, and no one could place them better,_ and I have taken the liberty to submit mine. What I am urging is not so much that my views shall be accepted as that the government shall take up the question on its own responsibility and deal with it efficiently so as to bring about a change in the present undesirable conditions. If anyone has something better to offer than this proposal of mine, I shall be very glad to accept it; but the principle laid down in the first part of the section I have read, is one I certainly wish to see adopted and the only one that will be fair to all parties. My hon. friend from Portage La Prairie has stated several times that it was desirable we should deal justly with the railway companies. Well, we are not dealing unjustly with the railway company. We do not wish to deal unfairly or unjustly with them; but if an animal be killed, whoever killed it should pay for it. If a railway company should kill it, that company should pay for it. That is the principle laid down in this section which I should like to see incorporated in our legislation.

I have listened very attentively to the very able argument 80}
of my hon. friend from Portage La Prairie. I sympathize with him very much in the views he has advocated. As I understand he is the author of the law as it stands at present. It was upon his initiative that the statute of 1910 was accepted by the government.

I am not the author of that law at all, nor was it enacted on my initiative. Subsection 4 of section 294 substantially as it is to-day, was enacted at the instance	of my hon.
friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) some time before I was in this House. Two years ago I introduced an amendment which did not substantially affect the law. That amendment the government adopted, and it was useful in so far as it went. It went this far. Previously, under certain conditions, the railways were responsible for injuries caused to animals by their trains or engines. The amendment proposed and accepted by the government enlarges the classes of damages but not the conditions under which the company would have to pay. It did not affect the law as it substantially stood, and as, for all purposes, it stands yet.

What I submit is this. If an accident takes place and nobody is at fault-neither the company, nor the owners of the animal-the burden of the loss must fall upon the company. That is, I think, the way my hon. friend put his case. It seems to me that the law' at present goes very far towards embodying in the statute that very idea, and I do not think the Bill my hon. friend proposes at all improves it in that respect.
I do not contend that it does in that respect. I contend that should be the law. It does not affect that class of cases at all, but a much larger class of cases.

At present unless the railway company establishes that the animal killed or injured got at large through the negligence, wilful act or omission of its owner or agent or custodian, the railway company is responsible. If a claim be made by the owner of an animal, what is the defence which the company may make? The company cannot say: I am not at fault, I have complied with all the requirements of the law. The company is liable even if its gates were closed, its fences in order, and its cattle guards in good condition. The only defence it can put up is this: You, the owner, were at fault because your animal was at large, and there was no one to look after it. If the company were to say that its fences were in good order, such a plea would not be entertained by the courts.

You cannot escape .the law unless you can show that the man is at faulj, himself. All the issue under the statute as it exists to-day is not the conduct of the company, but of the claimant. If the statute were as my hon. friend suggests that would be reversed. The thing then in issue would be the conduct of the company, because this is the amendment of my hon. friend. The company will be liable.
Unless the company establishes that such animal so got upon the property of the company without the negligence of the company or the omission of any duty binding on the company.
I think on the whole that the existing law is preferable to the proposed amendment.
I do not think my right hon. friend can show a case where a company were made to pay, if they were not in default.

I think my hon. friend is wrong in saying that there are no cases like that suggested by the right hon. the leader of the opposition. There is the case of Parks vs. the Canadian Northern railway, where it was decided that the company had no fences, not being bound by law to fence, but they were still held liable on the very principle laid down by the leader of the opposition. It was decided by Chief Justice Mathers, and the decision was maintained on appeal, (18 Western Law Reports, page 118).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What was decided?

I think the question decided was that the company had not fenced, and were not bound by law to fence in that particular locality, but that under section 294 as amended they were liable. That must be the result of the law as it stands.
In practice there are very few cases where the company have not been negligent.

Such cases as I have mentioned may not be common, but they may and do happen. I quite approve of the principle laid down, but I think the hon. member may do well to take notice of the objection raised by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as well as that since raised. Both of these might be easily overcome. The objection raised by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), is a most serious one, and I think if section 254 is left as it is, it will secure everything sought to be brought about by this amendment. By section 254, subsection 3, it will bei seen that the duty is absolutely on the railway company, they must provide fences and guards according to the decisions; suffi-Sir WILFRID IAURIER.
cient fences means absolutely sufficient fences and guards that the animals cannot get over. My hon. friend would do away with that entirely. The establishment of a standard ' guard ' rests with the Railway Commission. The railway companies tell us they cannot invent a cattle guard that will be sufficient, and then, as there must be some decision, the result will be that a standard will be fixed that is not sufficient.
My hon. friend has put in something that he should not have put in. I think he will 'agree that if he wishes to get on with this . amendment the safe way is to drop out that entirely, and leave the section as it was. Then it will be a tolerably effective amendment, as it will provide against the greater part of the evil. I think he would be wise to deal with the other objection too, that is, to leave it in such a way that the company is still liable. It would be a case where, though neither party had been guilty of wrong-doing, still there is a less; and he says, and rightly says, that the railway company should bear that loss.
I am anxious for this Bill to go through. It is important that it should go through at this particular stage, for we have been waiting too long already. The member from Portage la Prairie admits that he did not frame this other clause of the statute of 1910. No doubt he thought himself that those amendments were sufficient at that time. But he will agree with mo that he is not infallible, and if he looks at this carefully he will admit that he has made two serious mistakes, but they can be easily rectified. It is largely a,question of cattle guards. The railway company states that they cannot invent cattle guards which will keep out stock. I am not prepared to admit that, though I am not an expert on cattle guards. But I notice that when people have to do a certain thing or suffer a loss, they generally do it; and I have no doubt at all of the ability of the railway company to invent a cattle guard that will keep out cattle, but I do not believe they will ever do it until they have to. Necessity is the mother of invention, and they can invent something that will be effective. The law says they must but they don't, and the law protects them in case they don't. No doubt the hon. member for Calgary is well posted in all the arguments that favour railway companies; but the fact is that while the legislature says they must, the legislature provides that they should escape the penalty in case they do not. It provides that the farmer should suffer damage if they fail to carry out the requirements of the law. I think that is unreasonable. If the company openly violates the law, why should some one else have to suffer damage in consequence? The company is openly violating the law. Although they say thev cannot carry it out, I doubt the correctness of their statement. They openly

violate the law, and the farmer whose cattle are killed suffers the damage. I think the House will agree that is not just. There is possibly a little prejudice against the contention of the farmer, raised, perhaps, by reason of the way this section is worded. It says that if a man is guilty of negligence or wilful omission, he should not have any remedy. But that is not the approximate cause of the damage. The party who is principally liable, should suffer the damage, and that is no doubt the railway company.
My hon. friend from Richmond, N.S., says that in his province it is not reasonable to expect that the farmers will keep their cattle enclosed all the time, it is usual to let them run at large. I know that in many parts of the west in the ranching country, you cannot carry on business in any other way than by letting them run at. large. Even in the farming country of Saskatchewan it is not possible for farmers continually to keep their cattle in such a way that they may not occasionally get at large through "the negligence or the wilful act or omission of the owner. Take the case of an ordinary farmer in Saskatchewan, where I understand the conditions best. I know a very large portion of the fanners in sections where railways are fenced do not generally enclose their lands. The other day the farmers of the west were given a little lecture by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the necessity of mixed farming. I do not think a lecture in this House is ever going to make the farmers of the west go into mixed farming. You must give them a reason for becoming mixed farmers, but if you tell them that they must not keep any stock around their place unless they keep their animals enclosed, then you are going to discourage mixed farming in the west. Even in cases where the farmers have their lands enclosed, it is not usual throughout the winter to keep their lands inclosed (all the time, or to keep their lands inclosed in such a manner that no animal can escape. On the open prairie the snow drifts badly, and it is practically impossi-. ble to keep a gate so clear of drifts that you can open and close it every time you go through. As a matter of course,, that gate will be left open some time in the winter, and an animal may get at large. I hope that this House will be satisfied with the arguments that have been given, and acknowledge that it is only fair-play that we are asking. I hope that my hon. friend will consider the suggestions that have been given, and will agree to correct his amendment where it is at fault.

Possibly there may be a grievance in the west that requires amendment, or requires something in the way of
amendment. I am afraid that if this Bill were to pass as it has been drafted, the people in eastern Canada, where the railways are fenced, would be in a worse position than they are at the present time. It seems to me that the law as laid down by the Act of 1910 is almost ideal, so far as ordinary conditions are concerned all over Canada. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the conditions of farming in the west to know whether there are large portions of land that are not fenced, according to section 254 of the Railway Act. But in all eastern Canada I am satisfied that the railways do fence, practically in every case, according to the provisions of the Railway Act. Now the underlying principle of the amendment of 1910 is that the farmer can get paid unless the railway company proves that he is negligent, or guilty of wilful omission in leaving the cattle at large. If we adopt the principle laid down in this Bill we are entirely reversing that, and we are saying that the company is not negligent if it can prove that it has complied with all the requirements of the law. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle so forcibly a railway company might say: We have provided fences four feet six inches high-*-

Let me draw my hon. friend's attention to this point: The Act as pointed out by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, makes the duty of the company absolute to prevent cattle getting on the track. Their fences must be such, and their cattle guards must be such. If it is the case that they do not prevent them from getting on how can they get on except through the negligence or omission of the company?

I cannot understand that because they do get on and under the law, I do not care what the company may say, if the animals do get on the companv is liable, unless they can prove an act of negligence on the part of the owner.
That is prima facie evidence against the company. .

Yes, and in my practice I find that it works admirably. I have not had any difficulty in compelling the company to pay in every case where animals have been killed on the track. I am afraid that if the proposed Bill became law I would not be in the same position. I have no doubt whatever that if the animals got on the track the company would say: Our fences were all right, and our cattle guards are of the most approved pattern, it is not our fault, we have done everything we ought to do, and therefore, yon have no right against us. My hon. friend, I presume, has had some experience with railway conmanies. Railway companies keep their fences and cattle

guards in order through the agency of their workmen and officials, and you will never find a section man admitting that his fence or cattle guard is at fault if he can help it. Just as sure as a case goes to court under this Bill, you will find that it will not only be _ the wish, but almost the life of the section man or official, to say:	Our
cattle guards and fences are in perfect condition, which raises at once a question of fact and if the judge or jury decides that, [DOT]as a matter of fact, the cattle guard or fence was in proper condition, the farmer loses. The hon. gentleman desires to provide for a condition of affairs in the west, but, in so far as affairs in the east are concerned, I am satisfied that it would be a misfortune to the farmers if this Bill were made law and I think, that unless I can get some light upon it, I would be almost compelled to vote against the second reading.

My hon. friend says that he has always succeeded in making the company pay. Can he tell the House of a case where the company has been made to pay in which they had not violated this Act, in which they lived up to the provisions of this Act, and if so, would he give us the particulars?

I may say that I have not been compelled to sue the company since this Act was passed, but I have already collected a number of claims. I have collected half a dozen claims from the Canadian Pacific railway since this Act became law, and all I have been compelled to do, has been to prove that the cattle were on_the railway track and were killed.

Then, if you did not
have any cases yourself, could you give us the particulars of a case in which cattle were killed where the company lived up to the Act?

Not long ago I had a case where five sheep got on the railway track. I do not know by what agency, but the fence was torn down and the sheep got on the track. They paid. It may have been some outsider who broke the fence down.
They were in default.
No.
Yes, they must maintain a fence that will keep out the sheep.
My hon. friend is begging the question.
That is the Act.

If my hon. friend wants to get at the right side of this question let him direct his attention not to section 294 but to section 254. It would appear that there is a great deal of misconception on the part of the legal profession and rail-Mr. CARVELL.
railway companies as to what is meant by subsection 4 of section 254, with regard to fencing the line. When must the railway company fence? I think that the railway company should be compelled to fence every mile of its road and that it should take the same precaution through wilderness land as through cultivated land. I think that if my hon. friend would direct his attention to this section and make it obligatory upon railway companies to fence their track in every place and under every condition and leave section 294 as it is he would meet the difficulty. He would not be creating a condition of affairs which would be beneficial to the people of the west and against the interest of the people of the east, but he would be creating a condition which would benefit everybody and it would not be sectional legislation. Unless I can get some further light I am afraid I will be ' compelled to vote against the second reading of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot pretend to approach this question from the standpoint of the lawyer. I will have to leave that to the many eminent lawyers who are here and who can take care of that end of it, but I may make a few remarks and produce some little evidence in the shape of letters from some settlers that the present system in the west is no protection whatever to the farmer. Under the Saskatchewan law it is not illegal for cattle to be at large. I have never heard that it was; in fact, they are encouraged to be at large. The farmers there have accepted a law called the fence law. They recognize that it is better for their cattle to be out on the vacant land getting the grass, they are willing to protect their crops and to do that they are required under law to erect what is called a legal fence and to maintain gates. They are willing to do that; otherwise they cannot collect for any damage which may be inflicted upon their crops. I think that the railway companies should be obliged to protect their property in tire same way not only for the benefit of the farmers but in the interest of the travelling public because many wrecks have been occasioned by animals getting on the track. Under the present law they have to fence their railway, but I think it would be far better if there were no fence at all because the cattle get on the track with the present style of cattle guards. The cattle get over these guards and are entrapped. The fences are very good generally and the cattle guards are very poor. They get in between these fences, a train comes along, the animals are frightened and they run backwards and forwards and cannot get out. If there were no fences at all they would get out on the prairie again. Without better cattle

I have read these letters from some farmers that I know personally, as evidence that a great many cattle are killed. I think the Bill would be satisfactory except for the rider. I do not wish to say one word reflecting on the Railway Commission, which everybody in the west highly appreciates; but it seems to me that the official who passed the present cattle guards did not act on very good judgment. The Bill reads:
Such fences, gates and cattle guards shall be suitable and' sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway lands.
If it stopped there, it would be all right; but it goes on to say:
And the style, construction, material and dimensions of such cattle guards shall, before the 1st day of April, 1912, be submitted to the board and receive its approval.
There is no reason to expect that the Railway Commission would alter its judgment very much, so that we would be very much as we are at the present time. With that rider in the Bill, I think it is utterly use-

less, and, therefore, I cannot support it. I think, however, that something should be done in this matter. If the railway companies are not able to protect their tracks properly, I think they should pay for the damage, and there is no doubt they are able to do so. The Intercolonial railway does so, and the railways in the west should do so too. I have known people who could not put in their crops because they lost their horses on the railway tracks. It may be said that they should not let them run at large; but that does not relieve the railway company of responsibility. I have heard of a few cases in which the railway company made some allowance to the settler, but without prejudice. This i's a very important matter, but I do not think this Bill would give any relief.

I hope that what has been said to-night will convince the right hon. the Prime Minister that some action is necessary this session, and I am sure that other members of the House, like myself, who have Bills before the House to amend the Railway Act, would be very pleased to waive their rights to have those Bills considered until a consolidated Bill is introduced next session, so as to allow the Bill of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) to receive the consideration of the government at this session. We have heard to-night of the tremendous loss of money to settlers in these cases. I know of a case in my own constituency in which four horses which were being watered by the owner at his well ran on the railway track and were all killed, and he has never been able to collect one cent from the railway company. The loss practically put him out of business, the horses could not be replaced for $1,000. I think the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) is trying to get up something that will improve the Act, but after the explanations made by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), I am sure the House will see that if we leave clause 1 as proposed by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), we shall not accomplish his object. If it is provided that the railway company may get the endorsation or approval of the Railway Commission for its cattle guards, it will still manage to escape all liability. What we want to do now is to make the railway company liable for any animals killed on the tracks. If that is done the railway companies will very soon find means of preventing horses and cattle from getting on their tracks. In looking over subsection 4 of section 294 of the Act, it seems to me that it would be made all . right if the following words were omitted from it:
Unless the company establishes that such animal got at large through the negligence or wilful act or omission of the owner or his agent, or of the custodian of such animal or his agent.
If these lines were omitted, responsibility would be placed on the railway companies for every animal that is killed, except the ordinary exceptions such as the farmer leaving his gate open purposely, and there would not be one animal killed where there are ten killed to-day. The railway company should pay the loss, simply because in that case it is the general public that would be paying. If you make the railway company responsible, it will take the necessary means to prevent cattle getting on the track, and there -would be one killed in the future where ten or twenty have been killed in the past.
I hope that the right hon. the First Minister, w'ill see his way clear to make an exception in the case of the Bill of my hon. friend from Portage La Prairie. I am satisfied that if the hon. members for Portage La Prairie, Calgary, Edmonton and Qu'Appelle, were to get together for an hour, they could bring in a Bill that would be satisfactory to every one, and would gu through the House with very little discussion.

As I have some practical experience in this matter, 1 should like to say a few words concerning it. That some amendment should be made to the Railway Act which would give the farmers compensation for horses and cattle killed by railway trains is certainly of great urgency and importance to our western country. 75 per cent of the horses and cattle killed by railways, have been killed after they gained access to the right of way across cattle guards. A number of years ago, when Alberta was much more of a ranching country than it is now, an arrangement was made with the Canadian Pacific railway by which that company agreed to pay for all cattle-they did not include horses-killed or injured by their trains, without any necessity on the part, of the owners to take action against the company. But as soon as the Canadian Pacific railway had fenced in its right of way, that arrangement was withdrawn, and more cattle are being killed in southern Alberta by the railway trains to-day than before the right of way was protected When the right of way was open, Alberta was a great ranching country and cattle were free to roam over the prairie, and the accidents were far less in number. But since the putting up of cattle guards, the cattle frequently stray across these guards. Then, especially at night, they are dazed by the glare of the locomotive headlights, and unable to get off the track before they are struck. Whereas before the railway

tracks were fenced in, the cattle were in
no danger of finding themselves enclosed within the cattle guards, and had a greater stretch of clear space in which to escape. Within the last two years, a farmer in my constituency has lost eight fine horses, killed by the Crowsnest Pass railway, and received no compensation. The Canadian Pacific railway repudiated all liability, and under the law a conviction was almost impossible. There is one thing certain, and that is that the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners of a cattle guard put up by the company will not make it any the more efficient. If the company were compelled to pay the value of all stock killed which had crossed its cattle guards and gained access to the right of way, we should probably find much less loss in that connection than we do at present.
