House in Committee on Bill (No. 9) to amend the Criminal Code.-Mr. Stevens.
On section 1,
There have been some slight amendments in the Bill as at first introduced.
Do I understand that it is intended to drop line3 17 to 19, which describe certain particular kinds of lumber at least in eastern Canada that a man could take without being liable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The effect of the Bill is that shingle bolts are added to the list of the varieties of lumber and the waters of the coast are added to the lakes and rivers now included. The Act applies to the case of timber marked with an owner's mark. The only amendment in that regard is that the mark that constitutes a prima facie case against the person retaining the timber, is a mark under the Canada Timber Act, or a mark under the British Columbia Timber Act.

The law clerk has asked me to have this formal clause added:
This Act shall come into foroe sixty days after it has been assented to by the Governor General.

I have no objection to this Bill in that it does not go far enough. It provides for any log which is marked with a mark duly registered under the provisions of the Timber Marking Act, or of the statutes of the province of British Columbia. Now in New Brunswick, in practically all of our large rivers, we have what are called log driving companies incorporated by the legislature, to whom is entrusted the driving of logs coming down the river, and the different owners of logs register with the driving company the marks which they claim. Now the mark itself does not give them the prima facie title in the property which the Timber Marking Act does; but it is a fact that this law shows that the log is the property of the company, or of the person claiming the mark. It seems to me that this section might be extended to cover any mark which is well known as the property of the owner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law as it now stands attaches this privilege of constituting prima facie evidence of ownership exclusively to the marks that are registered under the Canada Timber Marking Act.
Them why add British *Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because there is a law in British Columbia which provides for that registration, and which is more generally used there. Now we are extending it to make it apply to brands registered under the legislation of _ the province, and if there be similar legislation in another province then it would be an analogous case. 3 understand the hon. gentleman to suggest that we should extend that to apply to the mark of every private company. I think this is a provision which is relieving an owner who comes to claim his property of the burden of Droving that which, in common law, falls upon him, and makes the particular designation mark prima facie evidence of his ownership. He would have to begin by proving registration of that mark, he would have to prove that that mark was his mark, which would be proving ownership. The purpose of the registration as it stood without this amendment was to attach to the registered mark, registered under the Dominion law, the privilege of making prima facie case against the man in possession of the log that he knew that mark, and, therefore, knew that he was getting somebody else's property. I think there may be a similar effect making a prima facie case of knowledge on the part of a man if he is in possession of a log bearing a mark which is registered under a law in force in the province. I think we may fairly expect a man to know the registered marks that are registered under a law of his province. But it might not be equally fair to throw upon everybody the knowledge of what is the mark of a driving company.

I appreciate the argument of the Minister of Justice. The fault I have to find with the section is that it either goes too far or not far enough. It creates a special law by the legislation of British Columbia, it creates a special right in some way in the legislation of British Columbia which does not apply to the legislation of other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will say that New Brunswick has a timber marking^ registration Act under which the registration of marks is provided for in a manner to be made public, I would say that we ought to include it. But I do not know of such an Act in New Brunswick, or in any of the other provinces. The hon. member who is promoting this Bill, does know of the existence of such an Act
in British Columbia, and the logs there are habitually marked by that mark which is registered and made public under that law.

There is no law in New7 Brunswick providing for the. registration of timber marks, but there is a law providing that the owners of lumber should register their marks with the driving companies, and then they get certain rights in the property. It amounts to the same thing in the end. It seems to me like sectional legislation, which applies to one province and not to all.

The Minister of Justice has been talking about the law of British Columbia, and the law of New Brunswick. But there is another part of the country, the province of Quebec, where a great quantity of pulpwood is cut and exported, and which is not marked at all. For instance, there is a concern who practically run all their logs on the river, and only a very small percentage are marked with a registered stamp. What will happen to the mill owner if the log is not marked at all ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Merely that these gentlemen will remain under the common law, and they will have to prove th,at these are their logs. This Bill only goes so far as to say that a registered mark will be prima facie evidence of ownership. It is attaching a privilege to the existence of a registered mark. I think it would be an extreme measure to say that any man who is found in possession of a log should be presumed to know that it belongs to somebody else, and would have to say where he got it. A man placed in that position might have had a log that did not have that mark upon it, and inasmuch as it is an unmarked log it would be just as hard to prove that it was his log, as for the man who claimed it to prove that it was his.
I have had some experience, and I know that there is a general impression amongst the public that if a man finds a log without a mark he has a right to take it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in this Act justifying that.
It may probably lead to some trouble in some places.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend would find it very hard if I walked into bis establishment, and he happened to have a large quantity of logs on hand, and I said: Those logs are all mine unless you prove that they are yours. My hon. friend suggests that it would be a good law that would entitle me to walk into his place and say: You prove that all those logs are yours or else I will prosecute you for steal-

ing them. I do not think we could go ns far as that.
